World.title: Dozens of attacks in southern Thailand wound three people
World.content:
Many local government offices and several vehicles were damaged or destroyed in the 51 attacks late on Saturday, according to the Internal Security Operations Command.

Dozens of coordinated arson and incendiary attacks across Thailand’s south left at least three people wounded and government property burned, the military has said.

Multiple local government offices and several vehicles were damaged or destroyed in the 51 attacks late on Saturday, according to the military’s Internal Security Operations Command (ISOC).

“Multiple coordinated incidents aimed at creating unrest occurred in various locations across the southern border provinces” from about 8pm (13:00 GMT) to midnight on Saturday, the ISOC said in a statement.

Firefighters worked to extinguish burning tyres left in the middle of a road and flames inside a 7-Eleven convenience store on Saturday night, while police officers stopped motorists for security checks, footage from the local broadcaster Thai PBS showed.

Most of the attacks were in Narathiwat province, where three civilians were wounded and an overnight curfew was imposed, while other attacks occurred in neighbouring Yala and Pattani provinces, authorities said.

Since 2004, a low-level conflict has simmered in the southernmost provinces of Buddhist-majority Thailand, killing more than 7,000 people, as rebels in the Muslim-majority region battle for greater autonomy.

No group has claimed responsibility for Saturday’s attacks.

Two women, aged 45 and 46, and a 21-year-old man were hurt in a roadside bombing in Narathiwat, provincial officials said in a statement.



All three were admitted to hospital and were in stable condition.

The national railway operator temporarily suspended part of a route in Narathiwat after officials found damage on the tracks “caused by a disruptive bombing incident last night”, the ISOC said.

Narathiwat Governor Boonchuay Homyamyen told local media that concerned agencies were investigating sites of the attacks on Sunday, including a local government office, telecommunications towers and electrical poles.

The Narathiwat military command earlier announced a curfew from Saturday night until 6am on Sunday.

A vehicle was stolen from the office of a subdistrict administrative organisation in Narathiwat during one of the attacks that left the building in flames, the ISOC said.

The burned-out pick-up truck was later found abandoned on a road.

Expected attacks

At a municipal office in Pattani province, damaged in another attack, army commander for the southern region Norathip Poinok said on Sunday that the assailants had aimed to destroy the building and undermine public trust in the state.

“We had intelligence reports for about two months that there would be attacks on local offices,” he told reporters, adding that the military had issued warnings to security agencies but did not know when and where the assaults would occur.

Rebels in the far south regularly carry out attacks on security officials and government property, including before visits by officials to the region.

Last month, assailants killed five soldiers in a shooting and bomb attack at a checkpoint in Narathiwat.

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and members of his cabinet are scheduled to make a two-day visit to the city of Hat Yai in southern Songkhla province next week to discuss investment projects, flood prevention and security issues, his office said on Saturday.

Formal talks between the Thai government and the National Revolutionary Front, abbreviated as BRN in the local language, the main separatist group in the south, were expected to resume in June after a rise in violence. The negotiations have struggled to resolve disagreements over self-government, security measures and political representation.

Earlier this week, Thanut Suvarnananda, head of Thailand’s National Intelligence Agency who was appointed by the government in April to lead the peace process, said he wants to move away from a transactional approach.

Thanut said he seeks to turn the BRN from an adversary into a potential partner in addressing demands from communities across Thailand’s deep south, including the predominantly Malay-Muslim provinces of Pattani, Yala and Narathiwat that were once part of the independent Malay sultanate of Patani.

World.title: Zelenskyy says wartime elections could ‘destroy’ Ukraine
World.content:
The embattled Ukrainian president slams Mykhailo Fedorov’s idea as a ‘tsunami’ that would ‘split’ the country.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has rejected his ex-defence chief’s calls for a wartime election, calling the prospect a “huge risk” amid the more than four-year war with Russia.

Ukrainian law bans elections during wartime, a measure that had gone unchallenged until former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov made the first public demand for a vote earlier this week.

Zelenskyy rejected the call during a wide-ranging briefing with reporters on Saturday.

“I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk. Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine,” the president said in comments published on Sunday.

“If we want to destroy the country, then we can move in the direction of elections during these times of war,” he added.

The 35-year-old Fedorov – a popular figure in Ukraine – held his post for just six months until Zelenskyy fired him in July, prompting protests across the country.

On Tuesday, he posted an explosive nine-minute video on YouTube claiming that Ukraine’s democracy “cannot be held hostage by Russia”.

“Can Russia actually be entitled to define when Ukrainians can elect their authorities next time? I’m sure it’s not,” he said, adding that Kyiv faces a “systemic crisis of governance”.

Experts have told Al Jazeera, however, that any wartime election would be practically impossible amid logistical and safety challenges, a reality that most Ukrainians agree with.

Kyiv tackles missile launchers, Starlink

Zelenskyy’s domestic political crisis is playing out as his government seeks more ways to curtail Moscow’s deadly air strikes.



Overnight Russian strikes in the eastern Donetsk region killed two people and wounded two others on Sunday, Ukraine’s emergency services said on Telegram. At least 141 private homes sustained damage in the attack.

Another eight people, including a child, were wounded in a drone attack on the northeastern city of Kharkiv that burned at least two residential buildings, the service said.

Meanwhile in the Odesa region, a Russian drone hit a passenger train travelling from Zhytomyr to Odesa, the Kyiv Independent reported, citing Ukrainian Railways CEO Oleksandr Pertsovskyi. No casualties were reported.

Amid the attacks, Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Ukraine is especially focused on hitting Russian ballistic launchers as Moscow ramps up its use of missiles – which effectively can only be destroyed by US-designed Patriot systems.

Ukraine has received just 264 Patriot missiles in 2026, down from 364 in 2025 and 675 in 2023, he said.

“When our antiballistic missiles are minimised – here is another tactic … hunting their nearby locations from which ballistic missiles are launched,” Zelenskyy said.

Ukraine is seeking to produce Patriot missiles domestically after receiving political blessing from United States President Donald Trump.

The Ukrainian president also said Moscow and Kyiv are building their own versions of Starlink, the satellite system used for battlefield communications that is controlled by US tech billionaire Elon Musk.

Russia’s alternative, developed “together with the Chinese”, is expected to be operational by December, Zelenskyy said.

He added that Ukraine would not “just sit and wait for Russia and China” and was “implementing a similar project with a European country”.

Funding gap

Ukraine’s wartime efforts may be hampered by a $27bn defence funding gap this year, Zelenskyy said, following defence spending that was higher than expected in the first half of 2026.

Ukraine needs at least $8bn for “a normal start” to 2027, he said, in addition to about $20bn more for other spending such as military salaries and payments to families of the dead.

Ukraine has reached an agreement with France for at least one SAMP/T air defence system this year, Zelenskyy said, and with Germany on the supply of about 600 PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors through 2028.

⁠Norway said on Sunday it would give 85 billion crowns ($9.2bn) to Kyiv for the 2027 fiscal year, in line with what it provided in 2026.

World.title: Can Iran retaliate against countries that join US ‘economic war’?
World.content:
Iran warns that countries backing US economic sanctions will be considered an enemy of Tehran.

Iran has threatened to retaliate against any country that joins the United States’ “economic war” against it, as diplomatic efforts to end the months-long war have stalled and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has drastically decreased.

The warning from Iran’s top security official on Saturday came as the US plans to announce new sanctions on Monday that could further strain the struggling Iranian economy.

So, how can Tehran retaliate?

Here’s what we know:

What has Iran said?

On Saturday, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told the IRIB state broadcaster that Iran was appealing to all countries around the world, including its neighbours, not to join the US’s “economic war”.

“Any country that takes part in imposing economic restrictions on us will be regarded as an enemy,” he said, warning of “seismic” retaliation.

Rezaei also warned Iran’s neighbours that if they participated in Trump’s economic warfare, “not even a drop of oil” would leave the Gulf region, including by alternative export routes away from the Hormuz chokepoint through which a fifth of global oil and gas exports pass in peacetime.

Iran has attacked US military installations and civilian locations since the war began on February 28 , on the pretext that Tehran was on the verge of having nuclear bombs. That claim was debunked by the US intelligence agency, as well as the UN’s IAEA nuclear watchdog.

The US operates military facilities in more than a dozen locations across the Middle East and North Africa, including in Gulf nations, such as Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Thousands of US soldiers are also stationed across the region, including in Jordan.



Rezaei’s remarks came days after US President Donald Trump announced that his government would undertake the “most crushing economic operation” yet against Iran. He also pledged “tremendous economic consequences” for any country that gives Iran “any type of lifeline”.

The US Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, echoed his threats the following day, saying, “You’re either with us or against us”. He also urged cooperation from China, which buys more than 80 percent of Iran’s oil shipments.

On Sunday, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said: Iran is “in a full-scale economic, military and security war” with the US. He said Washington falsely predicted before the war that it would fall amid US aggression and become like Venezuela.

“The enemy had assessed that if Iran falls, it will become Venezuela,” he said in a televised speech.

“Not only did it not happen, but it became a power that amazed the world with its resistance, solidarity and cohesion.”

How can Iran retaliate?

Rezaei described Iran’s strategy as a three-stage sequence, starting with talks with countries cooperating with the US to de-escalate tensions.

“Of course, we will first negotiate with them. We will hold talks and tell them to step aside and distance themselves from the United States.”

“But if they do not act, we will strike. We will target that country’s interests,” he added.

Rezaei’s warning that alternative export routes outside Hormuz could be targeted, probably points to the Bab al-Mandeb Strait gateway to the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia has used it to export its oil following the blockade of Hormuz. Tehran imposed a blockade on Hormuz in response to the US war and has since used it as leverage in negotiations with Washington to end the war. The US has put Iranian ports under a naval blockade, impacting Tehran’s international trade.

Hamidreza Azizi, a researcher on Iran at the Clingendael Institute, said in a post on X on Saturday: “Tehran appears to be trying to establish deterrence at an earlier stage, by signalling that even preparations for an attack could trigger an Iranian response.”

Azizi said two elements in the new “offensive doctrine” are emerging: preemption, which is aimed at preventing a perceived threat from materialising; and disproportionate retaliation, which is aimed at raising the cost of any attack that does occur.

Iran’s warning to Gulf states joining Trump’s economic war is “essentially an ultimatum” to the Gulf states, he said, adding that Iran’s military-security establishment “is increasingly preparing for another round of escalation”.



Will Iran’s neighbours join the US in its economic warfare?

Gulf countries, which are Iran’s neighbours and also US allies, have increasingly been finding themselves caught in the middle of the war. So it is unclear if they will join Washington in economically threatening Iran further.

Iran’s attacks on Gulf nations have impacted their economies, which use Hormuz for most of their exports, including oil and gas.

While Gulf nations have condemned Iranian attacks on their territories, analysts say Gulf states closely aligned with Washington recognise that a functioning political relationship with Iran is necessary due to its close proximity.

The UAE restored diplomatic relations with Iran in 2022 but imposed a trade embargo last week after accusing Tehran of a missile attack. Iran denies responsibility.

Saudi Arabia and Iran agreed to normalise ties in 2023 under a deal brokered by China, both likely a calculation that engagement with Iran was safer than permanent confrontation.

While the Iranian attacks on Gulf states have tested this idea, they have not necessarily shattered it.

“Ultimately, Gulf countries can’t change geography. They have to live and work alongside Iran,” Simon Mabon, a professor of international relations at Lancaster University told Al Jazeera in an interview last month. “They don’t want the instability that would come from the fall of the Islamic Republic. I think some Gulf states have pushed for harder strikes – not to precipitate its collapse, but to weaken the more hardline elements of the IRGC.”

Also last month, Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, told Al Jazeera that confidence in diplomacy to end the crisis remains low but, at the same time, no nation in the region “can afford another long war”.

As a result, that “will keep them away from a completely uncontrolled level of escalation”, and depleted global oil inventories will make a prolonged confrontation between the US and Iran unattractive.

“All inventories have not been able to be replenished” during the ceasefire, Parsi added. “We are at a much lower level globally.”

What we know about international sanctions against Iran over previous decades?

Since 1979, Iran has faced sanctions from the US and other nations in the West. The United Nations has also imposed sanctions on Tehran.

The US first imposed sanctions after the 1979 Islamic Revolution that toppled the pro-Western ruler Reza Shah Pahlavi. Washington said that was in response to Iranian students taking Americans hostage at the US embassy in Tehran.

Washington also halted oil imports from Iran and froze $12bn in Iranian assets following the revolution. Iranian products were banned from import into the US, apart from small gifts, informational material, foodstuffs and some carpets.

In 1995, President Bill Clinton issued executive orders preventing US companies from investing in Iranian oil and gas and trading with Iran. He banned US trade with Iran and investment. A year later, the US Congress passed a law requiring the US government to impose sanctions on foreign firms investing more than $20m a year in Iran’s energy sector.



Then in December 2006, the United Nations Security Council, whose members include China, Russia, the UK and France, imposed sanctions on Iran’s trade in nuclear-energy-related materials and technology and froze the assets of individuals and companies involved in related activities.

The sanctions were mainly an effort to curtail Iran’s growing nuclear capacity, but while programmes to enrich uranium were stopped in 2002, they restarted in late 2005. In subsequent years, the UN toughened the sanctions and imposed more. The European Union also followed suit.

In 2015, Iran signed a nuclear deal – the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) – with the US, EU, China, France, Germany, Russia and the United Kingdom. The deal put a cap on Iran’s nuclear programme in return for the complete lifting of sanctions.

However, in 2018, during his first term, Trump announced the US withdrawal from the nuclear treaty and reimposed all sanctions on Iran that were lifted under the treaty as part of his “maximum pressure” campaign against Tehran.

In 2019, the Trump administration designated Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) a ‘Foreign Terrorist Organisation’. Additionally, he imposed sanctions targeting petrochemicals, metals (steel, aluminium, copper) and senior Iranian officials.

During Trump’s first term, Qassem Soleimani, the head of the IRGC’s elite Quds Force, was assassinated in a drone strike in Baghdad in 2020. The US also imposed additional sanctions on Iran.

The Biden administration, in power from 2021 to 2025, kept in place most US sanctions.

Last September, UN sanctions were reimposed due to Iran’s nuclear programme when the UNSC voted against permanently lifting economic sanctions.

World.title: Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has said Canada wants "the benefits of being a State, without being one" after trade talks between the two countries collapsed late on Friday.

In his first comments since negotiations broke down, triggering new 50% US tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, Trump also said American farmers had been charged "massive amounts of Tariffs" for years.

It comes after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called the fresh tariffs a "miscalculation" designed to "hurt and divide us".

Carney confirmed he would match Trump's tariffs "dollar-for-dollar" from 8 September, including levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. The US and Canada are now in a trade "war", he said.

"They asked too much and they offered too little," Carney said on Saturday. "You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," he added.

Trump's latest comments echo his repeated references to making Canada the "51st state" of America since returning to office, sparking frustration among its leaders and residents.

The collapse of the trade talks upended a deeply integrated trading relationship, with no clear path to resolution.

"We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked," Carney said.

Both countries were optimistic of a deal earlier in the week, but talks fell apart after both sides accused the other of making last-minute changes.

The new 50% US tariffs will apply to a range of Canadian goods, in addition to existing US tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber.

They are limited in scope, covering about $20bn (Â£15bn; C$28bn) of Canadian imports, or about 5% in total, including wine, dairy, cement, clothing and hockey equipment.

The prime minister said Canada was retaliating "reluctantly" to protect its interests. Details of the counter-measures will be released in the coming days, he said.

World.title: Zelensky should be asked what he knew about government corruption, sacked minister tells BBC
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky should be asked questions about corruption in his government, his sacked defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has told the BBC.

Fedorov, a popular minister who modernised the military and pioneered drone warfare, was fired last month after reportedly falling out with the head of Ukraine's armed forces.

He told the BBC a money laundering investigation announced last week meant Zelensky should be asked about his awareness of potential corruption in his inner circle.

But he said he had not himself seen the president engage in any corrupt activity.

"In all the time that I worked with him, not a single time have I received from him any task or assignment that would go against law or my sense of integrity", Federov said.

The former minister also repeated his appeal for elections to be held in Ukraine, days after releasing a video where he called for a wartime vote.

"Democracy should not be the hostage of Putin", he said - but stopped short of declaring his own political ambitions.

There were angry protests over Fedorov's sacking but his support dwindled and demonstrations ended on Wednesday, after his replacement was confirmed. His call for a vote has been widely rejected.

Asked whether he missed his old job, the 35-year-old replied "No", citing the relentless stress of managing Ukraine's war with Russia while transforming its defence ministry.

Ukraine has been under martial law since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, meaning elections are suspended. Zelensky's five-year presidential term ended in May 2024.

But Fedorov said it was his "moral right" to start the conversation about elections.

"We should not be afraid of discussing it. That's what democracy is all about. If I cannot share my ideas and be open about them with my own society, then what are we fighting for?"

If elections were never held, he said, "then we are no longer a democracy".

World.title: DR Congo and M23 rebels agree roadmap for peace talks
World.content:
The Democratic Republic of Congo government and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group have agreed a roadmap for peace talks.

In a joint statement after five days of talks in Switzerland, they said they had pledged to "pursue negotiations towards comprehensive peace and conflict resolution" and set up a mechanism to monitor the ceasefire.

The roadmap sets out a timeline for talks under a US-brokered peace framework which they signed in 2025 - only for fighting to then continue in eastern DR Congo, which has been engulfed in conflict for decades.

But disagreements remain over issues including sanctions against M23, the release of detainees and the timing of political reforms.

The latest negotiations were attended by M23, the government of DR Congo, Qatar, the US, the Republic of Togo, the African Union Commission and host Switzerland.

"The parties agreed to establish a mechanism tasked with reviewing progress and addressing challenges in implementation of obligations and commitments under the Doha Framework Agreement," the statement added, referring to the 2025 deal.

They developed "sequenced steps and timelines" while also committing to "flexibility and creativity", the statement said.

They also agreed to implement a mechanism to monitor ceasefire violations. Its secretariat has been established and the first verification mission is due to take place on Monday in Minembwe, an area of South Kivu affected by fighting.

Fighting has continued in North and South Kivu despite repeated ceasefire commitments, with the government and M23 accusing each other of violations.

World.title: Dozens of co-ordinated arson attacks hit southern Thailand
World.content:
More than 50 co-ordinated arson and incendiary attacks "aimed at creating unrest" have been carried out across Thailand's insurgency-hit south, the Thai military has said.

At least two people were injured, with a local government office building, a convenience store, and a stolen vehicle among the targets set on fire.

The incidents took place across the country's southern border provinces between 20:00 local time (13:00 GMT) and midnight on Saturday, the military's Internal Security Operations Command said in a statement.

Most were reported in Narathiwat province, with others occurring in neighbouring Yala and Pattani.

According to the Bangkok Post, two women were injured when a bomb exploded in Muang district in Narathiwat province.

Telecommunication towers were set on fire in several locations, and security officials warned residents not to touch suspicious objects.

Authorities imposed an overnight curfew in the Narathiwat province that was lifted on Sunday morning. No further attacks had been reported on Sunday.

World.title: The hotel booking mix-up that could free mushroom murderer
World.content:
Last July, hundreds descended on Australia's Gippsland region from around the country for the most exciting event on the annual table tennis calendar.

But as elite players vied for medals at the national championships, one of the biggest criminal cases in the nation's history - that of mushroom murderer Erin Patterson - was unfolding just a few kilometres away.

This tournament inadvertently became part of a perfect storm which the triple killer's lawyers are now arguing "fatally undermined" the fairness of her trial.

The jury which condemned Patterson to prison were supposed to be isolated - sheltered from the frenzy surrounding the case while they deliberated.

But accommodation shortages in the region, exacerbated by the table tennis competition, meant they shared a hotel with members of the prosecution, a key police witness, and journalists.

Now Patterson's legal team is trying to overturn her convictions on appeal.

"The only proper remedy is... the order for a re-trial," Patterson's barrister Richard Edney said.

World.title: 'New season, new trim' - Haaland reveals buzzcut
World.content:
Whether it be Zlatan Ibrahimovic, Gareth Bale or Erling Haaland, football has witnessed some iconic man buns over the years.

However, Haaland has decided to begin the new Premier League season with a new - and very different - look.

The Manchester City striker revealed on social media that he had shed his famous blonde locks, posting the caption: "New season, new trim."

Haaland will be hoping his new look brings even more goals as he aims to get off the mark when Enzo Maresca's side face Bournemouth at 14:00 BST on Sunday.

Before cutting his hair, Haaland joked around by showing off some images of his previous hairstyles during his career, and some questionable ideas of how his new hair should look.

Looking nervous as the hairdresser cut the first piece, it didn't take long for Haaland to start smiling about his new appearance.

There were mixed reactions when the 26âyearâold made video calls to City team-mate Jack Grealish, Oasis' Noel Gallagher and former City manager Pep Guardiola.

Gallagher said: "You look about 17 years old. It's good. Change is good."

Grealish and Guardiola both said they "love" the change.

"You look about 10 years old. That is hilarious. I can't stop looking at the front of your hair. I love it," said Grealish.

"No way. You're lucky you have hair. I would love to have it. I love it," said Guardiola.

Before calling Ibrahimovic, Haaland joked that the former Sweden international told him never to cut his long hair.

"Zlatan told me, never cut your hair, because your strength is in your hair. I'm a bit nervous. I want a buzz cut, like in the military."

It turned out Ibrahimovic was not impressed that Haaland didn't follow his advice.

"What did you do? You lost a bet or what? Block me and erase my number," Ibrahimovic said.

World.title: Golf brand apologises for advert that shows woman being pushed over
World.content:
Content creator and golf brand Good Good has apologised and removed an  for a new golf driver which showed a woman being pushed to the ground after reaching for the club.

American company Good Good, which has 2.13m subscribers to its golf channel on YouTube and sponsors a PGA Tour tournament, had created and published the advert for golf club manufacturer Callaway.

The advert drew a backlash and was accused of making light of violence against women.

"We posted a video to our channels that ultimately depicted actions that are not aligned with our values as a brand," read the Good Good apology on X, external.

"We have since taken that content down, and sincerely apologise.

"Good Good has always stood for making the game of golf more inclusive to all, and we will continue to ensure that is our mission moving forward".

The advert showed Good Good co-founder Garrett Clark rushing over to Alexis Miestowski - a professional golfer and regular content creator for Good Good - and pushing her to the ground before shouting: "Do not touch my new driver."

World.title: Kejelcha breaks men's half marathon world record by 29 seconds
World.content:
Ethiopia's Yomif Kejelcha has broken the men's half marathon world record, winning a World Athletics road race in Buenos Aires on Sunday in 56 minutes 51 seconds.

The 29-year-old previously held the record with a time of 57:30, set in Valencia in October 2024, but lost that to Uganda's Jacob Kiplimo in March.

Kiplimo ran 57:20 in Lisbon earlier this year but Kejelcha has now knocked 29 seconds off that time to regain the record, subject to official ratification.

The world track silver medallist in the 10,000m also holds the world record for a men's 10,000m road race.

He also became one of the first men to run a sub-two hour marathon in record-eligible conditions earlier this year when finishing second behind Kenya's Sebastian Sawe in the London Marathon.

Sawe won the record-breaking race in 1:59:30, beating Kejelcha by just 11 seconds.

World.title: Call me Tony: A parable of corporate Nigeria, By Temitope Lakisokun
World.content:
The awkwardness lies in the system itself: a borrowed convention that was designed to soften hierarchy but was never properly reconsidered as the generations changed… The lesson is not that young Nigerians must learn to fear their elders. It is that modernity does not require us to forget why certain social conventions existed in the first place. We are not “oyinbo.”.. Respect can coexist with equality just as much as warmth can coexist with formality.

The argument over the young trainee who addressed UBA Chairman Tony Elumelu by his first name has become a surprisingly revealing debate about Nigerian society.

One side says she was disrespectful. The other says she did nothing wrong: UBA has a first-name culture, and she followed it.

I think both sides are looking at the wrong thing.

The question is not whether she should have said “Good morning, Tony.” It is why a convention that once seemed progressive and liberating has become so awkward when applied across generations.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The answer has something to do with second-order thinking.

First-order thinking asks: What is the immediate benefit of this change?

Second-order thinking asks: What happens because of the change? And what happens after that?

Nigeria has never been particularly good at the second question.

Consider the case of the civil servants who Murtala Mohammed dismissed in 1975. They had spent their careers in government service, accumulating little beyond their salaries and quarters, no private property, no cushion against sudden displacement. Most had no reason to steal; they worked diligently because they trusted that government would honour its side of the bargain. But when the dismissal came, many were left destitute, their years of service counting for nothing. The lesson was not lost on those who survived the purge. They saw what happened to their senior colleagues and concluded that loyalty was no protection. If government could discard them at will, they had better secure themselves while they could. They saw what loyalty had cost their predecessors and resolved that they would not suffer the same fate. That was the day Nigeria’s corruption problem found its institutional footing. A straight line runs from that moment to the present.

The Great First-name Revolution

Sometime in the corporate culture of the 1980s and 1990s, a number of Nigerian executives began importing ideas from American business schools and corporate America, most of them fresh from a three- or four-week course at Harvard or Yale, which, by a happy coincidence, was just enough time to be thoroughly convinced of everything!

Among the ideas that arrived was the notion that hierarchy should be softened by having people call one another by their first names.

It made sense at the time.

Nigeria’s corporate culture could be excessively deferential. The distance between Oga and subordinate made honest conversation difficult. Junior employees might hesitate to challenge senior executives. A first-name culture promised to make the workplace less intimidating.

For a time, it worked. Most executives were peers in age and experience. Calling the managing director “Tony” or “Fola,” did not erase hierarchy; everyone still knew who held what position. The informality simply sat on top of an already understood structure. Everyone felt a little more modern, and y’know, more “with it.” This was the early ‘90s version of performative modernity.

The trouble began when time did what time always does.

The contemporaries became elders.

Then their children joined the organisations.

Now, their grandchildren are arriving as graduate trainees and interns.

It’s safe to say the old convention has encountered a circumstance its original architects had not really considered.

Imagine a chairman in his mid-to-late sixties addressing a room of young trainees. Some of them are young enough to be his grandchildren. The corporate rule says: “Call me Tony.”

The society outside the office says: “This is your elder.” So, which instruction is the young person supposed to follow?

That is the real problem and the fence nobody asked about.

GK Chesterton’s famous argument about the fence is useful here.

If you encounter a fence in the middle of a road and cannot see why it is there, the sensible response is not immediately to tear it down. First ask why someone put it there. Perhaps the fence is unnecessary. Perhaps it is protecting something you cannot see. Either way, you need to understand its purpose before removing it.

Social conventions are often like that.

A title may appear unnecessarily formal, but such conventions often perform a social function that becomes invisible, precisely because they have worked for so long.

This, in my opinion, is what the Nigerian corporate first-name revolution failed to consider. It borrowed the visible feature of another culture without necessarily considering the social system around it.

America’s informal corporate culture did not develop in a vacuum. It sits within a particular history of individualism, social mobility, and attitudes toward authority.

For centuries, Nigerian societies have attached meaning to age, seniority, office, lineage and relationship. The language of respect was one of the ways society organised itself.

A younger person knew how to address or greet an elder. A subject knew how to address a king. A junior knew how to address a senior. An apprentice knew how to address a master.

These distinctions did not necessarily mean that one human being was worth more than another. What they did was establish relationship. Unfortunately, relationship is the thing the first-name convention can obscure.

Respect Is Not the Same thing as Servility

There is an understandable desire among younger Nigerians to reject the old culture of Oga and Madam, particularly when those titles are used to demand obedience, rather than to acknowledge legitimate authority. That criticism is fair because respect should never become a licence for humiliation. But the answer to excessive deference is not necessarily the elimination of every marker of seniority.

The French still distinguish between “tu” and “vous.” Japanese language has “san” and a much wider system of honorific speech. These societies have modern economies, sophisticated corporations and highly educated young people. They have not concluded that acknowledging social distance is incompatible with modernity.

But here in Nigeria?!

Social hierarchy must disappear because “we woke.”

If UBA’s established culture is that employees call one another by their first names, then it is difficult to pile on the young lady. She may have done exactly what the institution taught her to do.

And that is precisely why the incident is more revealing than a simple story about an impolite young Nigerian.

The institution created the convention, which the employee followed.

The convention then produced a result that many people instinctively felt was wrong. Should that not make us examine the convention, rather than simply blame the individual?

The original intention may have been useful in reducing unnecessary distance between people. But second-order thinking asks what happens when that convention is carried forward for thirty years.

A policy designed by contemporaries for contemporaries has now encountered a new generation, and a well-intentioned corporate convention has become an albatross.

The Deeper Nigerian Problem

This is not really an argument for returning to an age of rigid hierarchy.

It is an argument for thinking before we dismantle things.

Nigeria has a habit of importing institutional ideas because they appear modern, without asking what assumptions make them work in their original setting. We inherit the form without understanding the function. A whole lot of, (ahem) religious practices come to mind here.

This is what Chesterton’s fence is about.

Before removing an old convention, ask what it was doing. Before telling every Nigerian employee to call every senior person by his or her first name, ask one very simple question:

What happens when the chairman is old enough to be the intern’s grandfather?

That question should have been asked thirty odd years ago.

The awkwardness lies in the system itself: a borrowed convention that was designed to soften hierarchy but was never properly reconsidered as the generations changed.

The lesson is not that young Nigerians must learn to fear their elders. It is that modernity does not require us to forget why certain social conventions existed in the first place. We are not “oyinbo.”

Respect can coexist with equality just as much as warmth can coexist with formality.

And perhaps the next time we encounter a Nigerian convention that seems old-fashioned, we should resist the reflex to tear it down simply because someone in Boston, Palo Alto or at Harvard Business School does things differently.

First ask:

Why was the fence built?

Temitope Lakisokun, a political consultant, and Chair of Trustees of the Tarihi Trust Foundation, writes from Lagos.

World.title: Hope for cancer patients as scientists report breakthrough in personalised cancer vaccines
World.content:
Researchers in the United States have reported promising results from a personalised cancer vaccine designed to prevent melanoma from returning or spreading.

The vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, is being developed by Moderna, a biotechnology company, in partnership with Merck, a biopharmaceutical company.

It is designed for patients with high-risk melanoma after their tumours have been surgically removed, Reuters reported.

According to the National Cancer Institute (NCI), melanoma is less common than other major types of skin cancer but is more likely to invade nearby tissue and spread to other parts of the body. Most deaths from skin cancer are caused by melanoma.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The American Cancer Society estimates roughly 112,000 new cases of invasive melanoma and 8,510 deaths for 2026.

Merck and Moderna said the vaccine helped prevent the return and spread of melanoma in a large trial involving more than 1,000 patients. The patients had localised tumours that had been surgically removed but were considered to have a high risk of recurrence.

More about the vaccine

The treatment combines a personalised mRNA vaccine with Merck’s immunotherapy drug, Keytruda.

Unlike chemotherapy, which kills both healthy and cancerous cells, personalised cancer vaccines are designed to train the immune system to target mutations specific to a person’s tumour, Reuters reported.

The treatment uses up to nine doses of Keytruda, given every six weeks, together with up to nine doses of a customised mRNA vaccine. The vaccine is designed based on the specific mutations in a patient’s tumour and instructs the immune system to attack the patient’s cancer cells.

Merck describes intismeran autogene as an “mRNA-based individualised neoantigen therapy” designed around the unique mutational signature of a patient’s tumour. The company said it uses synthetic mRNA coding for up to 34 neoantigens.

Neoantigens are features of cancer cells that can help the immune system recognise and attack them.

What the trial found

Merck and Moderna said earlier five-year data from a Phase 2b trial showed that adding intismeran autogene to Keytruda reduced the risk of cancer returning or death by 49 per cent, compared with Keytruda alone.

The combination also reduced the risk of the cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 59 per cent, according to Merck.

Ryan Sullivan, director of the Centre for Melanoma at Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute, described the findings as “a big deal for the field in general.”

“With this positive study, there is hope,” Sullivan told Reuters, adding that the approach could change the way cancer is treated more broadly.

The Chief Medical Officer of the American Society of Clinical Oncology, Julie Gralow, described the trial results as “a monumental leap forward,” saying they validate mRNA technology as a cancer treatment.

Elizabeth Buchbinder, a melanoma specialist at the Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute, said melanoma was chosen for testing partly because it produces many mutations, making it easier for the immune system to identify.

Buchbinder said many other cancer types also produce multiple mutations, suggesting the approach could have broad applications.

“We’ll see, but it’s definitely an ​area that is going to be exploding, especially with these results coming out,” she was quoted as saying.

More cancers being studied

The research is already moving beyond melanoma. Reuters reports that Moderna and Merck are conducting trials of the treatment in other cancers, including non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer and kidney cancer.

The companies are also studying the approach in pancreatic and stomach cancers, with results from several trials expected over the next one to two years, Moderna President Stephen Hoge told Reuters.

Other companies are also developing similar mRNA cancer vaccines. Roche and BioNTech are testing a similar treatment, known as autogene cevumeran, in patients with colon and pancreatic cancers who have undergone surgery.

“We should be hearing results from multiple studies over the next few years, and there’s every reason to hope now,” Robert Vonderheide, president-elect of the American Association for Cancer Research, said.

However, the current melanoma trial is still ongoing, and the companies have not released the full results. Researchers will continue to follow participants to determine whether the treatment also extends overall survival.

In January, PREMIUM TIMES reported that Spanish scientists had eliminated pancreatic cancer tumours in laboratory mice using a combination of three drugs.

The researchers, however, stressed that the treatment had not yet been tested in humans and that further validation and safety testing would be required before human trials.

World.title: MOVIE REVIEW: ‘God when?’ goes wrong in Funke Akindele’s ‘Where Is Mr Right?’
World.content:
Singles and the prayer ‘God When?’ are like a pair in a pod. Inseparable they may seem, but for many single people, the longing for love, companionship and marriage can sometimes turn into desperation, leading them to make choices they might otherwise avoid.

It is this familiar struggle that Where Is Mr Right?, the romantic comedy directed by Tunde Olaoye, explores.

Produced under the Funke Akindele Network, the film stars Funke Akindele alongside Omowunmi Dada, Bisola Aiyeola, Blossom Chukwujekwu and Nosa Rex (Baba Rex). It premiered on Prime Video on 15 August 2026.

At its heart, the film asks a deceptively simple question: what exactly makes a man “Mr Right”? The answer, as the film gradually suggests, may have less to do with the checklist people construct and more with the person who can genuinely connect with them.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Plot

Bomi is a successful event planner and the CEO of Big Surprises, but despite her thriving career, one thing is missing from her life: marriage.

Unlike her two married sisters, Bomi is still single and desperately wants to find her own Mr Right. She admires happy couples, follows marriage counsellors, attends programmes at church, and even dresses as though she is already preparing for her wedding, hoping her miracle will come sooner.

Every morning, Bomi watches a seemingly perfect couple, Bridget and Temi, jog together around her estate. Their loving relationship becomes the picture of the marriage she dreams of having.

When Bomi becomes friends with Bridget, she unexpectedly meets Bridget’s younger brother, who develops an interest in her. Just when Bomi believes her long-awaited love story may finally be falling into place, her happiness is shattered when she becomes entangled in a shocking murder case.

What begins as a desperate search for love soon turns into a journey filled with secrets, unexpected twists, and big surprises that force Bomi to question everything and everyone around her.

Review

Where Is Mr Right? struggles not to be constrained by the typical Nollywood romance format, introducing intriguing twists, including suspense, crime-thriller elements, and irony.

For instance, following Temi’s death, the movie offers the audience a departure from the Rom-com narrative it had earlier set, giving them a run for their time and moving away from the straightforward search-for-love narrative.

For some audiences, the unpredictability gives the final stretch energy. For others, the transition can feel abrupt, particularly because the film spends considerable time establishing itself as a relatively familiar relationship comedy.

The problem is not necessarily the presence of a twist. Rather, it is how completely the film prepares the audience for the change in narrative. A stronger screenplay would have planted more clues earlier, allowing the eventual developments to feel inevitable in retrospect rather than simply unexpected.

Still, the willingness to take that risk deserves some credit. In a genre where audiences can often predict the destination long before the characters arrive there, unpredictability is valuable. Perhaps the most appealing thing about Where Is Mr Right? It does not present love as a perfectly organised formula.

What makes the movie relatable is the pressure to marry, the expectations surrounding social status, religious beliefs, family intervention, and the influence of social media. All these searches for a partner are considerably more complicated than the romantic-comedy cliché of simply “finding love”.

A film such as Where Is Mr Right? does not have to depend entirely on a long theatrical run to find an audience. Its accessibility to streaming subscribers also means that viewers can encounter it as a weekend watch, a date-night movie or simply a light piece of entertainment.

Where Is Mr Right is an enjoyable but imperfect romantic comedy that understands its audience better than it challenges it. However, the film is less convincing when it attempts to move beyond entertainment into deeper crime thrillers and the complexities of modern relationships.

For viewers looking for a light Nigerian romantic comedy with familiar faces, relationship drama and a few unexpected turns, the film is a reasonable streaming choice.

Verdict 6/10

Where is Mr Right is streaming on Prime Video

World.title: NDLEA intercepts cocaine hidden in fufu on boat bound for Cameroon
World.content:
A 27-year-old man has been arrested after operatives of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) allegedly found cocaine hidden inside a wrap of fufu on a boat heading from Akwa Ibom State towards Cameroon.

According to a statement by NDLEA spokesperson Femi Babafemi on Sunday, the suspect, Kingsley John, was arrested alongside two other men during the interception of the wooden boat on Friday, the agency said in a statement on Sunday.

The boat was allegedly heading towards Ine Isu, Ine Mbah and Ine Ikot Itie Udung, fishing ports in Cameroon.

NDLEA noted that Mr John had 20 grammes of cocaine concealed inside a large wrap of edible cassava flour. He was also carrying 435 grammes of skunk, a strain of cannabis.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The two other suspects were identified as Etima Effiong Eekpo, 29, and Otobong Eyoh Etukudoh, 33.

The agency said Mr Eekpo was found with 1.12kg of skunk, while Mr Etukudoh had 42.06kg.

In total, 42.622kg of illicit drugs was recovered from the three men.

The interception followed intelligence on the movement of the boat towards the fishing settlements in Cameroon, according to the agency.

The operation comes days after the NDLEA announced the seizure of 184.5kg of cocaine worth about N39 billion in Lagos.

That consignment, valued at about $27.7 million, was intercepted while being processed for export through a courier company, the agency said.

The seizure led to the arrest of two suspected members of an international drug trafficking network, including Afolabi Kazeem Michael, popularly known as KC Luxury.

The NDLEA Chairman, Buba Marwa, described Mr Michael as the Nigerian “arrowhead” of the alleged syndicate.

Mr Michael, a businessman and social media personality, was arrested on 13 August at the boarding gate of the Murtala Muhammed International Airport in Lagos, where he was about to board a business-class flight to Paris, according to Mr Marwa.

Operatives allegedly recovered €7,750, £2,800 and N100,000 in cash, as well as jewellery, from him.

The agency also searched his apartment on Banana Island, Lagos, where it said exotic vehicles and other assets were recovered.

Mr Marwa, a retired brigadier general, stated that the investigation showed that the syndicate allegedly moved cocaine from South America through Nigeria to the United Kingdom, Europe and Asia.

He said investigators were working with foreign counterparts and that some members of the network had already been arrested abroad.

The NDLEA explained that the Akwa Ibom operation was part of its efforts to stop Nigeria’s waterways from being used to move illicit drugs across national borders.

Mr Marwa commended the officers involved and urged them to sustain the crackdown on drug trafficking.

World.title: NDLEA arrests 101-year-old woman for selling cannabis in Ogun
World.content:
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) has arrested a 101-year-old woman for allegedly selling cannabis in Ilisan, Ogun State.

According to a statement on Sunday by the NDLEA spokesperson, Femi Babafemi, the woman, Esther Ogunmabo, was arrested on 15 August with 90 grammes of skunk, a strain of cannabis, packaged in small sachets, the agency said in a statement on Sunday.

During questioning, Ms Ogunmabo reportedly told NDLEA operatives that she took up the drug trade after a fire destroyed her provisions shop.

She said one of her daughters, who lives in Lagos, supplied her with cannabis every four days, which she then sold in small quantities.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Because of her age, the NDLEA Chairman, Buba Marwa, directed that the woman be granted bail and placed on counselling.

Her daughter was also arrested over her alleged involvement in supplying the drug.

The case adds to recent arrests by the NDLEA involving elderly Nigerians accused of dealing in illicit drugs.

In June, the agency arrested two men aged 84 and 75 in Umuahia, Abia State, for allegedly supplying illicit substances to secondary school students.

One of them, Godfrey Orji, 84, was arrested after security guards at Saint Silas Secondary School, Old Umuahia, reportedly caught him supplying drugs to two teenage students.

The other suspect, 75-year-old Godwin Obiora, was arrested at his patent medicine shop on Club Road, Umuahia, following intelligence that he was selling illicit substances to young people.

The NDLEA stated that 4.64kg of opioids, including tramadol and diazepam, were recovered from Mr Obiora’s shop.

A 15-year-old student allegedly told investigators that Mr Orji supplied him with drugs, which he used and also sold to other students.

The two students were subsequently placed on counselling and rehabilitation, according to the agency.

The statement also announced the arrest of a 65-year-old woman, Adebayo Kaosarat, in Ibadan, Oyo State, on Friday.

She was arrested at Akobo-Ojuirin with 1.795kg of Scottish Loud, 1.66kg of tramadol, 600 grammes of codeine syrup, 125 grammes of diazepam and 50 grammes of flunitrazepam.

Mr Marwa, a retired brigadier general, commended NDLEA officers involved in the recent operations and urged personnel across the country to sustain the agency’s efforts against illicit drug trafficking.

World.title: NDLEA seizes N4.4bn ‘Thai Loud’ at Lagos ports, uncovers new trafficking route
World.content:
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) has intercepted 1,490.5kg of cannabis, popularly known as Loud, worth more than N4.4 billion in two containers shipped from Thailand through the Apapa and Lekki ports in Lagos.

In a statement by the NDLEA spokesperson Femi Babafemi on Sunday, the seizures, made within days of each other, have drawn the agency’s attention to a new route being used to bring synthetic cannabis into Nigeria.

Both containers originated from the Port of Laem Chabang in Thailand, according to the NDLEA.

At the Apapa Port, NDLEA operatives, working with the Nigeria Customs Service and other agencies, examined one of the containers on Friday.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The import documents showed that the container was carrying dry fish, rice, vehicle spare parts, turmeric soap and inverter batteries.

The contents told a different story, according to the NDLEA.

The search uncovered 1,090.5kg of Thai Loud packed in 54 cartons containing 2,181 sachets, each weighing 500 grammes.

At the Lekki Deep Sea Port, another container had already been placed on the NDLEA’s watchlist and was being monitored by its Marine Special Operations Unit.

It was jointly examined on Wednesday, leading to the discovery of another 400kg of Thai Loud.

The drug was found on four of the seven pallets in the container, packed in 96 cartons containing 400 parcels.

The other three pallets held 798 reams of A4 paper, which the agency said had been used to conceal the consignment.

The two seizures brought the total quantity of Thai Loud recovered at the Lagos ports to 1,490.5kg.

The NDLEA said the interceptions were the first involving illicit drugs shipped from Thailand through Nigeria’s maritime corridor.

The development is significant because most large cannabis seizures announced by the agency in recent months have involved consignments from other countries.

On 20 July, for instance, NDLEA operatives intercepted 2,388.5kg of Canadian Loud at the Apapa seaport.

The drug was packed in 4,777 sachets and concealed in three vehicles. The agency put its street value at more than N7.1 billion.

The latest seizures suggest that traffickers are continuing to explore Nigeria’s busy seaports and different international supply routes to move synthetic cannabis into the country.

The NDLEA Chairman, Buba Marwa, commended the officers involved in the operations.

He urged them to maintain the pressure on drug trafficking networks operating through the country’s maritime corridors.

World.title: ‘Some people are trying to profit from my father’s illness’ — Ogogo’s daughter alleges
World.content:
Kira, daughter of veteran actor and screenwriter Taiwo “Ogogo” Hassan, has alleged that some people are exploiting her father’s stage four cancer diagnosis for financial gain.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that Kira and her sister, Haleemah, revealed in videos that doctors diagnosed their father with cancer and appealed to Nigerians to help the family explore possible treatment options, including traditional medicine, after alleging that a hospital had declined to treat him.

The sisters, however, clarified that the family was not asking Nigerians for money. Their appeal prompted offers of assistance from members of the public, including recommendations of hospitals and traditionalist homes where Ogogo could receive treatment.

His colleagues later said his condition meant he could not be moved from the hospital where he was receiving care.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Financial exploit

Speaking during a TikTok live session on Saturday, an emotional Kira, who broke down in tears, alleged that some people were using her father’s illness to create unreasonable videos, while others were seeking to profit from the family’s difficult situation.

She said, “Some people are saying different things, and some are trying to make money from this entire situation. Please fear God. For any little thing, Nigerians want to make money; please, take it easy. Because we said we are not looking for financial assistance does not mean you should drain us.

“Some people will say they have solutions that will cost ₦1.5 million. Another says ₦800,000. Another says ₦5 million. Another says $11,000. Another says $15,000. Please fear God. What is happening? What a pity.”

“A good father”

Kira further said she did not know how she would cope if anything happened to her father.

She described Ogogo as a loving father who prayed for everyone and always made sure those around him were fine.

“I do not know how I will feel or see the world again if anything happens to my daddy. I am not here to ask for sympathy; this is how I feel.

“If anything happens to my daddy, I do not think I will ever be okay again. My daddy is a good father. He wants to pray for everybody and make sure they are all right.”

“Is he going?”

Kira also said videos circulating about her father’s health caught the attention of her “big daddy”, who asked whether Ogogo was going to die.

She said the bond between her father and her “big daddy” was so strong that the children sometimes wondered whether the two men loved each other more than they loved their children.

Kira noted, “To those who made the video my big daddy saw, I leave you to God. After the video, he came into the group created to discuss my daddy’s health. I saw my cousin write something, and my big daddy was asking them whether Taiwo was already going. We, the children, do not know who my daddy and big daddy love more, themselves or us.

“My big daddy loves my daddy far too much to be asking whether Taiwo was already going. That question said everything. When everyone was calling me yesterday, I did not want to pick up or come on social media because I could not bring myself to look at my daddy’s picture. When I saw the message on the group chat, I simply left and turned off my Wi-Fi. That statement from my big daddy is a lot. I know he is not okay.”

Backstory

This newspaper earlier reported that Ogogo’s colleagues held a prayer session for him, seeking God’s intervention and recovery from cancer.

READ ALSO: Nigerian actors gather in prayer for Ogogo as he battles stage four cancer

They prayed for healing to reach the actor wherever he was receiving treatment and asked God to restore his health.

The prayer session followed a show of support from Ogogo’s colleagues after his daughters disclosed that he was battling stage-four cancer and could not travel abroad to seek treatment.

His daughters also expressed fears of losing their father, saying they were desperate to secure appropriate treatment for him as quickly as possible.

They added that Ogogo had repeatedly expressed his desire to live.

World.title: INTERVIEW: How Bajju Diaspora can transform development back home — Agwam Bajju II
World.content:
Since he emerged as the second paramount ruler of the Bajju Chiefdom in 2022, His Highness Luka Kogi Yabwat (Agwam Bajju II) has focused on strengthening the traditional institution, completing a permanent palace project, improving security and deepening the relationship between the chiefdom and its growing diaspora community.

During his recent visit to the United Kingdom, where he met members of the Bajju community and witnessed the launch of the Bajju UK and Europe Association, the monarch spoke exclusively to PREMIUM TIMES.

In this interview, the royal father discusses his priorities, the legacy of his predecessor, the proposed educational trust by the diaspora, security challenges, agriculture, investment, youth development, tourism and his vision for the Bajju people over the next decade.

PT: Since you came into power in 2022, looking back at your time on the throne so far, what would you describe as the defining priority of your reign?

Agwam Bajju II: Thank you for this opportunity. When I came in, my priority was securing permanent residence for the king.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

When I came in, I had a lot of problems with accommodation. The late king was not able to secure a permanent palace because he was living in his own house, so he didn’t put much effort into it.

One good thing he did was secure the land and start something. The foundation was laid.

So, building on that foundation, I continued with the committee that the late king appointed for the palace project. I called them and set a time limit for them to secure a temporary residence for me while we worked on the permanent palace.

The timeline I gave them was not enough, so we had to extend it. Meanwhile, they had to find a temporary residence for me, which is where I am now.

From there, I continued working with the committee. It started in a simple form, but to the glory of God, both our sons and daughters are contributing to its completion.

As I am talking to you now, the building is at one stage. We are trusting God that in the next one or two years, we will have a permanent residence, which is my heart’s desire.

PT: Has the Kaduna State Government been part of the palace project?

Agwam Bajju II: We have never received any support from the state government. We have never received any support from the state government.

Even though we wrote to them about the project, we have not received any support to date. And I think it is not only the Bajju project. It is like that with most chiefdoms in the southern part of the state.

PT: Your predecessor played a significant role in establishing the identity and traditional institution of the Bajju Chiefdom. What lessons have you taken from his leadership, and what aspects of his legacy are you determined to preserve?

Agwam Bajju II: The late chief, whom I owe a lot of respect, actually worked hard to preserve the Bajju identity. He did a lot of things. He set the structure of the chiefdom.

So, by setting the structure of the chiefdom, I have not done anything different from what he had done because he had already set up everything that was needed. We are just trying to add one or two things.

He did a lot.

PT: The Bajju community has a large presence in the UK and across Europe. What role do you expect Bajju sons and daughters in the diaspora to play in developing Bajju communities in Nigeria?

Agwam Bajju II: To be sincere, that is why, when they invited me to come down, I was so happy that I was coming to meet my people, my subjects in Britain and Europe.

They have been very strong supporters of the chiefdom down there. They have contributed immensely to the position we are now in regarding the progress of the palace project.

We can say we are depending on them seriously. We are looking up to them.

The chairman is here. We are looking up to them. We are not just looking up to them; we are depending on them to lead.

My invitation to Europe, I think they have already taken the lead, and I am sure all the Bajju sons in the diaspora will follow suit.

PT: The Bajju UK and Europe Association has identified education as one of its priorities and plans to establish an educational trust for less privileged children. What is your vision for the fund, and what impact do you think it can have?

Agwam Bajju II: It will have a lot of impact. You see, any society that is not literate — I know that literacy could mean so many things — but any society that is not developed educationally is a backward society.

Their thought of establishing a fund for educational development is a welcome one. It will enable my people to rise. It will enable my people to meet the challenges of life.

So, I know that what they have done, the launch last week, was another welcome development that will impact my people, the Bajju and the Kajju, entirely.

PT: How can traditional institutions and modern democratic governments work better together to bring infrastructure and economic development to rural areas like Bajju?

Agwam Bajju II: The traditional institution plays a great role if only it is given the opportunity.

Traditionally, most of the things that promote the economy come from rural areas, and that is where traditional institutions are based.

So we encourage our people to engage in a lot of agricultural activities. It is farming and other activities that keep the economy going.

If only the government could support by providing fertiliser, herbicides and the rest, there would be a great change economically.

Secondly, at the grassroots, we are the ones being attacked. Insecurity is high at the grassroots.

If the government can come to the aid of the traditional institution, it will help us. If everyone can go to the farm freely, without fear of being attacked, it will boost the economy.

What we want is government support. What we want is for the government to enable us to stand on our own.

Because if there is no security, life is meaningless.

We are encouraging people, even with the insecurity going on, to get involved in farming, not only during the wet season but also during the dry season, so we can get food and other things that can sustain us.

We are working with the local government, the state and even the federal government. When they look for where to put one thing or another, they usually come to us. So we will do everything possible to ensure that they get what they are looking for.

PT: You mentioned security. Can you give an example of how traditional institutions and local security structures help protect communities?

Agwam Bajju II: It may amaze you to know that just this week, we had local hunters who were told that they saw some people in a certain location, unknown to the communities, and they were armed.

They passed the intelligence report to us. We passed it to the government, the police, the DSS, and the rest — and we mobilised local security.

When they attacked, we did not know that they had kidnapped three young girls and were hiding them in that location. But my own security, that is, the local hunters, were able to rescue them.

That is another aspect in which we worked with the government.

This has been the cry of everyone: that the federal government should work with local structures on security because local people know the terrain where the crisis is happening.

That is exactly what happened. They knew the terrain and knew where the people could be.

I was here when I coordinated the whole activity. It was a huge success. The people are jubilating. The people are happy with what we have done.

PT: What has been your most effective strategy for building and sustaining peace with neighbouring communities?

Agwam Bajju II: You know, I am from the correctional service, so I have experience in this area. I know what to do.

We organise meetings with the locals, district heads, village heads and ward heads. Even during security meetings, the security agents, the police, the DSS, and other relevant agencies are there.

We ask ourselves: what is happening in this or that district? They tell us, and then we start working on our intelligence system.

Sometimes it is not through meetings. Sometimes they just call us and say something is happening somewhere, and then we organise.

In the case I just told you, the police were there, but a large part of the operation was carried out by local vigilantes and hunters.

That is what we are doing, and God has helped us to achieve this success so far. I don’t joke with any security issue. Any security report, I take action because I know what it used to be.

PT: What specific role would you like the Bajju diaspora to play in security and community development?

Agwam Bajju II: They are here, and they are outside. Sometimes they tend to get information from home.

Since most of them are online, they may access information on security and other matters. What I want is that where they have information that we have not received, they should inform us.

That will enable us to do our homework and ensure that the people are secure.

PT: Apart from agriculture, what sectors would you like investors, particularly those in the diaspora, to explore in Bajju land?

Agwam Bajju II: There are so many areas where we want Bajju people in the diaspora to come in, especially those in the UK.

They can come in through cottage industries. All kinds of cottage industries can come in.

Even in agriculture, they can add value by processing some raw agricultural materials that are currently exported in raw form, especially ginger, soybeans, and others.

If they can come in through such small industries to add value to agricultural products, I think that would attract more investment.

PT: …And employment for the youth?

Agwam Bajju II: Yes, it would create employment for the youth. It would reduce crime. It would reduce crime. So that is what we actually want.

PT: Are there programmes in place to shield young people from radicalisation, drug abuse and crime?

Agwam Bajju II: Yes, that is why we are concerned. That is why the Bajju people are beautiful.

We sat down and agreed to control alcohol and these dangerous drugs that the youth are indulging in.

We formed committees. The district heads form committees that check those selling the drugs and those taking them.

It has been a remarkable success in that area.

Sometimes, when they go out to check where these drugs are sold, the police and DSS are there. We also work with other security agencies established by the government.

We work hand in hand with them to ensure that we bring the use of these dangerous drugs to the barest minimum.

Because it is from these dangerous drugs that they commit crimes.

PT: What cultural festivals or landmarks would you like the Bajju Kingdom to promote to the international community and researchers?

Agwam Bajju II: We have a Bajju Development Association that organises a festival every year. The one last year was very fantastic. We invited people from all walks of life.

That festival showcases all kinds of our traditional crafts and things that remind us of the past.

If the people in the diaspora could help, it would help make it more widely known.

We have a website with a lot of information about us and even the palace building. There are also many places that have been highlighted for tourism.

If you are travelling from Kaduna down south, you will notice that the air and vegetation are different. The land is very fertile for planting, especially during the rainy season, and there are certain crops that you can only find there.

There are also very beautiful granite rocks. They are still there. The place is very promising, and security is our main issue.

If we get security sorted, there is a lot of potential.

PT: Finally, what has been your feedback from this journey to the UK and your meetings with the Bajju diaspora?

Agwam Bajju II: I’ve seen unity. I’ve seen how they love the people back home, and that is why they invited the king to represent the entire kingdom.

What I saw here is something that hasn’t been done before. They showed us that they are with us, that we are together.

They showed us that even though they are far away, their hearts remain connected to the people back home.

This is one of the things, among so many others, that I saw. They took care of me. They have been so good.

PT: What do you hope to see in Bajju land in the next 10 years?

Agwam Bajju II: I hope to see much more than what I am seeing today because if they continue in this spirit, it is enough to change things back home.

When I came here, nobody was saying, ‘I’m from this village’ or ‘I’m from that village.’ That was not the issue.

They all came together from Britain, France, the Netherlands and Germany just to come and see the king.

I’m so proud of them. Honestly, it’s the first of its kind.

That is what we encourage them to do, no matter how small. There are textbooks on the language. We all learnt English, so the language can also be taught to the children.

I encourage them to get the books they can buy from home because they will go a long way.

I met one child whose parents speak the language fluently and are teaching her. They have been here for a long time. Her intonation has changed to English, but we manage it like that.

When they get back home, they won’t feel like strangers because their parents teach them.

The Yorubas are good at maintaining their language and culture, and I encourage the Bajju people to do the same.
