World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Fugitive swaps, a strawberry spat and a stronger peso
World.content:
Mexico and the United States spent the week of Aug. 17 trading shows of security cooperation, from fugitive handovers to a new drone-technology pact, culminating Wednesday in a federal operation in Michoacán that saw nine alleged members of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel arrested and set off narco-blockades at more than 20 points across the state.

That cooperation ran alongside friction on other fronts. Mexico is contesting a proposed U.S. antidumping tariff on strawberry exports and objecting to Washington’s decision to deport some Mexicans to Central America rather than home, as trade uncertainty lingers more than a month after the U.S. declined to renew the USMCA free trade deal in its current form. Domestically, the fallout from the U.S. visa revocation of former president López Obrador’s son continued to shadow the government’s messaging on fuel-smuggling enforcement. Against that backdrop, the peso’s push below 17 to the dollar stood out as a rare point of good economic news, as the central bank held its interest rate steady on lingering inflation concerns.

The week also brought a new Mexico-made electric vehicle, a national debate over kids and social media, and a presidential sick day. Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Fugitive returns and a new drone pact mark security cooperation

Mexico and the United States kept up a steady drumbeat of security announcements this week. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said U.S. authorities returned three wanted fugitives to Mexico in a single day — one linked to the CJNG, one wanted for murder in Zacatecas and one for fraud — while separately handing over six more fugitives wanted for crimes including murder and firearms offenses. Jalisco police also captured Antoni Covarrubias, wanted for second-degree murder in California, in Puerto Vallarta, which Johnson called the ninth high-profile U.S.-targeted arrest in the state in recent weeks. At the same time, the U.S. and Mexico conducted a joint security exercise along the El Paso-Ciudad Juárez border, and the two countries signed a declaration of intent on drone technology that will let Mexico’s Defense Ministry access the U.S. Army’s marketplace for unmanned aircraft systems, though no models, quantities or purchases have been agreed.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch drew public praise from DEA Administrator Terry Cole at the 40th International Drug Enforcement Conference in Buenos Aires, where García Harfuch said U.S. agencies are processing 155 arrest warrants tied to Mexican investigations and reported that Mexico’s Financial Intelligence Unit has frozen more than 8.6 billion pesos in assets. He also cited a more than 50% drop in daily homicides, from 86 to 42, over the past two years, a figure attributed to his ministry’s own count of arrests and seizures.

The Michoacán operation capped the week’s security news: Soldiers and National Guard troops arrested nine people, including two women identified as relatives of CJNG plaza boss Heraclio “Tío Lako” Guerrero Martínez, who evaded capture as the operation set off blockades that were largely cleared by Wednesday afternoon.

That flow of cooperation announcements ran alongside a separate dispute over fuel smuggling and politics. Sheinbaum said at Tuesday’s mañanera that fuel smuggling, or huachicol fiscal, is “practically over” in Mexico thanks to customs interventions and arrests — a claim she offered in the context of defending her government against opposition criticism. That criticism stems partly from the U.S. revocation of the visa of Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, son of former President López Obrador, which Sheinbaum has called a political matter, saying he “was not” ever on authorities’ radar for criminal involvement. The fuel-trafficking case itself advanced this week when Rear Admiral Fernando Farías Laguna, accused of leading a Pemex-linked smuggling ring, was extradited from Argentina and jailed at the Altiplano maximum security prison. The case has damaged the Navy’s reputation and drawn indirect allegations, which Sheinbaum has rejected, involving López Beltrán.

Strawberries, Vietnam imports and a Canada call test trade ties

Mexico is contesting a U.S. Commerce Department finding that could impose antidumping tariffs on Mexican strawberries, which supplies 98% of U.S. strawberry imports. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard called the U.S. criteria “arbitrarily applied” and inconsistent with USMCA provisions; a final ITC ruling isn’t expected until early 2027, and the case could affect roughly 5,000 Mexican producers and 151,000 jobs if it proceeds. Sheinbaum has warned the case could set a precedent for challenging other Mexican agricultural exports.

Separately, Mexico’s imports from Vietnam more than doubled in the first half of 2026 to $18.4 billion, a jump that has raised suspicions — flagged in a recent White House report naming Mexico a “Tier 1” transshipment risk — that Chinese goods are being routed through Vietnam to dodge Mexico’s tariffs on non-free-trade-agreement countries. Mexico has denied being a transshipment hub for Chinese goods bound for the U.S.

Against that backdrop, President Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney discussed North American trade by phone on Thursday. Carney’s office said the two underscored the importance of renewing the USMCA pact soon, and separately thanked Mexico for deploying more than 400 firefighters to help combat wildfires in British Columbia. The call came as Trump-imposed tariffs on Canadian goods, delayed this week, loomed for Saturday absent a deal. (The U.S. tariffs on Canada ultimately went into effect after trade talks collapsed late Friday night.)

Peso strength collides with a cautious Banxico

The peso dropped below 17 to the U.S. dollar this week, dropping below 16.9 on Friday, largely on dollar weakness following a U.S. Treasury bond buyback announcement. The currency has appreciated nearly 6% in 2026, a gain Banxico credits with helping cool inflation.

Even so, the central bank held its benchmark rate at 6.5% earlier this month. In meeting minutes released this week, four of five board members cited persistent services inflation as a driver of that decision. Headline inflation slowed to 3.12% in July, but Banxico now doesn’t expect it to reach its 3% target until the fourth quarter of 2027. The bank also flagged Middle East tensions as an upside risk to oil prices. Separately, INEGI’s preliminary July data showed the economy growing 2.7% annually, which Rodríguez called “another piece of good news” following 2.1% growth in the second quarter.

Other business and finance news this week:

Mañanera themes: EVs, phone lines and a presidential sick day

On Monday, Sheinbaum said she opposes a social-media ban for minors like Australia’s, calling the idea “very problematic” and noting enforcement challenges, while Education Minister Mario Delgado announced a nationwide teacher consultation on classroom device rules ahead of the Aug. 31 school year.

At Thursday’s press conference, Sheinbaum unveiled a prototype of Olinia Carga, the government’s second domestically developed electric vehicle, a light-cargo EV that can carry 650 kilograms and will sell for around 150,000 pesos starting in late 2027. The same day brought a new arrest in the 2024 kidnapping case of Sinaloa Cartel figure “El Mayo” Zambada.

On Friday, Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez, standing in for an ill Sheinbaum, told U.S. Ambassador Johnson that Mexico disagrees with Washington’s decision to deport some Mexicans to Guatemala, Honduras and Costa Rica rather than to Mexico.

Elsewhere, millions of Mexican cell phone lines were suspended after an Aug. 15 mandatory registration deadline passed, though regulators say most affected users can still recover service. Mexico also abstained from an OAS vote, which passed 29-1, to convene an emergency session on Nicaragua’s move to bar opposition candidates, with representative Alejandro Encinas citing Mexico’s non-intervention principle. Friday’s mañanera, run by Rodríguez after Sheinbaum announced she had the flu, also touched on new archaeological finds in a Chiapas cave tied to Zoque ritual traditions.

Regional news roundup:

And some good news to close out the week:

Looking ahead

Several threads left open this week are likely to develop further: Security cooperation with the U.S. continues to strengthen, while trade friction between the two countries shows no sign of easing. On a practical note, cell phone users facing the next registration deadlines — Aug. 31 for numbers ending in “1” — should act before their lines are suspended.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: From the archive: How to whistle like a true Mexican
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in January 2025 — is a perfect example, offering humorous insight into the fine art of whistling.

I have known no jealousy like the jealousy I feel when I hear Mexicans’ elaborate category of effortless whistles.

Okay fine, they’re not effortless. They just sound that way because they learned how to do it when they were kids. You know, like speaking Spanish.

Indeed, whistling is part of the language in some meaningful ways. There are specific whistles used for getting people’s attention. There are whistles for saying “Hey buddy, what’s up?” from across the street. There are whistles for saying, “But of course, my horse” — okay, maybe not exactly that, but a kind of “You know it!” with that adorable tone. There are whistles to say, “Wowza, nice butt, strange woman I don’t know!” Some whistles say, “Okay, back up your car now, a little more, a little more, a little more, stop!” There are even whistles to tell people where they can stuff it. Careful with those.

And I am going to learn them all.

A realistic goal

Well, I’m going to try. Forget turning my health or finances around; it’s too big a task. I need something I actually stand a chance at being able to bite off. Even though the prospect of practicing them takes me back to the deep humiliation I felt trying to string a four-word sentence together in Spanish while the three-year-old next to me rattled off deep, complex sentence after deep, complete sentence, I’m committed. I did it once, and I can do it again!

I won’t necessarily use them all, or use them frequently. In fact, I’m fairly certain that men whistle much more than women around here, anyway. Like cursing, it falls into a decidedly “male” category of behavior, and is seen as somewhat crass and unladylike.

I’ve also noticed that whistling is more prevalent among lower socio-economic classes than among the more well-to-do. Part of this is simply cultural habit, growing out of the need to communicate at great distances. It’s more pleasant sounding, and clearer, than shouting. If you’re willing to do some digging, there are actually some fascinating examples of whistles-as-language. There’s a cool short video about this below.

But I don’t need to be communicating over great distances in the Oaxaca countryside. I just want to have some fun.

Indigenous Whistle Language In Mexico

Watch this video on YouTube

And I don’t want to go too fast, but I’m also an eager learner. This video is pretty cute, by the way, as an introduction to the meanings of different whistles.

Here are the specific ones that I want to learn:

Learning how to whistle in Mexico (in different styles, for different purposes)

The whistle to get someone’s attention

Say you’re walking along a busy street and you need to get someone’s attention. Maybe it’s a vendor, or maybe a taxi that didn’t notice you! This whistle is perfect for it. It’s also important for me personally, because my voice does not carry at all. My loudest is not very loud, and the strain on my voice physically hurts! This can either be a quick low-high sound, or the more universally recognized high-low-slightly higher.

The ‘you can count on me, buddy’ whistle

I mostly want to learn this one because I think it’s both hilarious and adorable. My partner does this one sometimes, and even though it’s kind of a joke, I am 100% charmed.

‘Hey, friend on the other side of the street!’

Finally, I’ve just got to learn this whistle. It’s short and sweet, and I don’t care that I’ve hardly ever heard it from a woman’s lips.

So those are the three goals. Three distinct whistles — I can kind of do a “pucker” whistle now, but not very well — should be manageable in a year, right?

In the meantime, I’m dying to know: can you whistle? Can you do any specifically Mexican whistles? I especially want to know how many women out there can — please let me know in the comments!

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Guadalajara residents turn to citizen science as water crisis deepens
World.content:
On a Saturday morning in Guadalajara’s historic Analco neighborhood, residents arrived at the Casa Bandera community center carrying bottles and jars filled with water from their homes.

At folding tables, researchers from ITESO, Guadalajara’s Jesuit university, showed them how to dip inexpensive reactive strips into the samples, wait for the colors to change and compare the results against a chart measuring pH, chlorine, lead, mercury and other indicators. Samples showing signs of possible bacterial contamination could undergo additional testing for E. coli.

It was the latest workshop in an expanding citizen water-monitoring network that has grown out of Guadalajara’s months-long water crisis — and out of residents’ frustration with what they see as inadequate information and action from the authorities responsible for providing safe water.

“We don’t claim to be scientific specialists or water experts,” Héctor Morales, one of the workshop presenters, told participants. “We are citizens contributing evidence from what we are observing and living through, and that is equally valid.”

“We’re not trying to compete with science,” he continued. “We’re trying to generate knowledge that comes from everyday life. That’s the approach of citizen science.”

Sunday: Mega March + Agua KK Fest

Guadalajara’s water activists will be having some fun with the theme at Sunday’s festival — without losing sight of the very serious problem behind it.

When: Sunday, Aug. 23

10 a.m.: Gather at Parque Rojo

11 a.m.: Mega March for Water departs along Av. Juárez

Noon: Agua KK Fest at Plaza Liberación

The workshops will feature home water filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets and water testing, plus children’s activities, music, decorated water jugs, costumes and karaoke. The cheeky Agua KK name is a play on the word caca — a pointed joke about the dirty water that residents say has been coming from their taps.

From complaints to citizen evidence

The network brings together neighborhood residents, scientists from ITESO University, the Mexican Institute for Community Development (IMDEC) and the citizen campaign #ElSiapaQueQueremos, or The SIAPA We Want — SIAPA being the city water utility.

The idea is not simply to tell residents what might be in their water. María González of IMDEC said the testing has two purposes: helping families take care of themselves, and creating a body of evidence that can be used to press authorities for action.

“This helps us protect ourselves. You are going to know what is in the water in your homes,” González told the group. But the results, she said, are also “our citizen evidence for legal action, for institutional action, for mobilization.”

Before Saturday’s workshop, the network had analyzed roughly 184 samples from 90 neighborhoods in five municipalities. Organizers said residual chlorine was found in only 12 of the 184 samples. That’s a problem, they pointed out. Chlorine is added during water treatment, and a small amount should remain as water travels through the distribution network to help protect it from bacterial contamination.

The monitoring also detected lead in 20 samples, fluoride in 52 and mercury in an unspecified number, according to Morales. Four of the 184 samples tested positive for E. coli, a form of fecal coliform bacteria.

The citizen findings are not a statistically representative survey of Guadalajara’s water supply, a limitation organizers repeatedly emphasized. The low-cost tests do not measure all of the dozens of parameters required under Mexico’s drinking-water standard.

“What does this analysis tell us?” Morales asked. “It tells us when the water is not safe. What doesn’t it tell us? It doesn’t tell us when the water is good.”

Certifying water as safe, he said, requires much more extensive laboratory testing.

Still, official testing has now documented some of the same warning signs.

In late July, Jalisco health authorities confirmed that E. coli had been detected in 18 of 297 samples analyzed between March and June in neighborhoods affected by water-quality problems. Officials also acknowledged insufficient chlorination in some areas.

The findings came after months of complaints about yellow, brown or foul-smelling water, as well as sediment and service interruptions across the Guadalajara metropolitan area. González said the #ElSiapaQueQueremos campaign has now received nearly 1,500 complaints, with water quality by far the most common problem, followed by outages and high rates.

A multibillion-peso response

The Jalisco government and SIAPA, the metropolitan water utility, have acknowledged serious problems in the aging system and announced a long-term overhaul requiring more than 20 billion pesos in investment.

Among the major projects are the replacement of the aging Chapala-Guadalajara aqueduct and the modernization and expansion of Potabilizadora No. 1 in Miravalle. Governor Pablo Lemus said this month that the federal government had agreed to support both projects.

But for the citizen coalition, repairing infrastructure is only part of the solution.

The movement is increasingly focusing on who participates in decisions about the water system, how information is shared and whether communities themselves can have a formal role in monitoring and oversight.

That shift will be on display Sunday, when the same groups organizing the monitoring workshops will hold a “Mega March for Water.” Participants will gather at Parque Rojo at 10 a.m. and march along Avenida Juárez to Plaza Liberación, where the deliberately scatological “Agua KK Fest” — a play on caca, or “poop,” in reference to residents’ complaints about dirty water — will begin at noon.

The festival will combine protest with workshops on household filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets, urban gardens, community water systems and water-quality monitoring. Organizers describe the event as peaceful, family-oriented and nonpartisan.

Beyond fixing SIAPA

The coalition’s demands now extend beyond cleaner water. Its latest statement calls for greater transparency, citizen participation in decisions over water quality, distribution and infrastructure, formal recognition of community monitoring and protection of the watersheds that supply the metropolitan area.

It also proposes “public-community agreements” that would bring SIAPA, universities, neighborhood organizations, workers and other sectors together to share knowledge and participate in water governance.

The organizers explicitly reject privatization as the answer to SIAPA’s failures.

“The alternative to an inefficient SIAPA is not a privatized SIAPA,” their statement says, calling instead for a public utility that is transparent, efficient and subject to democratic social oversight.

González said the campaign is also pushing for a permanent working group focused specifically on water quality, health and sanitary risks. Authorities have not yet agreed to participate.

But organizers do not intend to wait indefinitely.

The group, González said, “is going to be established with authorities or without authorities,” functioning independently if necessary to prevent health risks.

That determination reflects how far the movement has come since residents first began showing up at public meetings with bottles of discolored water.

Morales said citizen monitoring allows residents to reach places government agencies may not sample and to turn individual experiences into systematic evidence. He has watched workshop participants take what they learn back to their neighborhoods — and then into the streets.

“It’s beautiful to see people who come to the workshops later at demonstrations with signs saying, ‘There are nitrates and nitrites in our water,’” he said.

“The authorities never expected that.”

World.title: The story of Zarzaparilla, an Indigenous root beer from Veracruz
World.content:
Mexico’s truest beauty can often be found in its widely diverse, uniquely regional variations of culture and flavors. No two places in Mexico are exactly alike. Whether it’s the way a certain salsa is prepared, the protein of choice used to stuff a tamal or the techniques that may differ from coast to coast, pueblo to pueblo, the country reflects an endless multiverse of realities inside its kitchens. As a taxi driver in Oaxaca once told me while driving across the desert terrain, you can spend two lifetimes in Mexico and even then, you still wouldn’t uncover all of its secrets and taste all of its idiosyncrasies.

It was a revelation, then, when I learned about zarzaparilla — about its historic origins and regional importance — from one of my uncles who grew up in Veracruz. In the simplest terms, zarzaparilla (referred to simply as zarza by locals) is what modern consumers would likely associate with root beer. But centuries before making its way into European markets via the Spanish — who in the 16th century first encountered the Indigenous remedy in the mountains of what is now Veracruz, and then exported it to Seville, Spain — zarza was a native drink with purported medicinal qualities made from local roots and ingredients that combated syphilis and, according to the American Homebrewers Association, far predates root beer.

A root beer revelation

In an effort to learn more about it, I drove 45 minutes to the source, on a southbound road from my home in Veracruz past two Pueblos Mágicos — first Coatepec, then Xico — until I reached Mexico’s cradle of zarza: Teocelo (or, in Nahuatl, “Tiger God”).

The mountain town of around 11,000 can only be reached through narrow, curving roads that carve through the subtropical terrain at a high elevation — with humid and wet conditions that allow all sorts of vegetation and crops to flourish in the surrounding areas (coffee, in particular, is a notable product from this part of Mexico).

It’s here that zarzaparilla (also confusingly spelled “sarsaparilla”) gained notoriety as a beverage among Spaniards and mestizos, becoming a local commercial industry of sorts that would expand beyond the region. Today, zarzaparilla can be found throughout Mexico, particularly within Veracruz and its neighboring states. But back then, it was — much like jalapeños were until they became commonplace elsewhere — a specialty product known only to those in the greater Xalapa vicinity.

The origins of ‘zarza’

In snooping around the tiny pueblo, it’s easy to find where it all started: Zarzaparilla Flores (a family-owned business that is not to be mistaken for a separate branch of family operations, Zarzaparilla Flores Doña Chabe, which is literally next door, but technically unaffiliated). The original Zarzaparilla Flores is said to have opened in 1920 inside what used to be a storage building for the nearby train yard, which served as a prominent trade route during the Porfiriato era from Xico to the United States. Due to the train, lots of immigrants and outsiders were able to pass through town, bringing a transient mixture of passersby who helped give zarzaparilla its fame beyond Veracruz.

Today, a third-generation family member runs the business — with antique family photos dating back to the Mexican Revolution bedecking the walls (one photo of the original shop owner, Don Manuel Flores, and his wife hangs stoically beneath two old rifles).

Rubén Olivares is the current face of operations. He married into the Flores family and has taken over the zarzaparilla tradition with pride.

A family tradition and recipe

“This region used to be known for cultivating pineapples and oranges, and that created a local exporting economy early on,” Olivares says. “But over time, with climate change and different farming methods, everything shifted, and pineapple exports migrated further south, due to the hotter temperatures down there. And this area, which has always been colder and at higher altitudes, began to grow coffee and other ingredients that were good for making zarzaparilla.”

Without revealing the specifics of their family recipe, he tells me their zarzaparilla is a mix of ginger, cardamom, star anise, cinnamon, lime, jamaica, egg whites and more. They also sell hidromiel (mead) and other liquors made from fermented oranges, arrowhead plants, cherry and crucetillo (a shrub that in the past was used to treat venomous snakebites).

The family’s zarza recipe has remained the same for more than a century and was patented in 1920 by Don Manuel Flores, but according to Olivares, Don Manuel only sold a few liters of it at the time. The family now regularly brews batches of around 1,000 liters and ships it all over Mexico. Predominantly made as a syrupy concentrate, the molasses-like mixture is put into various sizes of plastic bottles and jugs, which consumers can mix with any ratio of filtered or mineral water to their liking.

How the drink conquered the ‘Wild West’

In the 19th and 20th centuries, the beverage was viewed as a medicinal remedy and was brought to the U.S. According to The Seattle Times, “Sarsaparilla was widely consumed all across 19th-century America, easy to find in the local saloon if the one-road town one rode into had no dedicated apothecary or pharmacy, and was supposedly quite popular with cowboys and ranchers looking to tame a rumbling tummy or put a little pep in their step, much as people use kombucha today.” Eventually — and it’s unclear when, why or how — zarzaparilla (made from “dried root bark of several plants in the genus Smilax,” which grew plentifully in Veracruz) was replaced by sassafras, and zarzaparilla became known as root beer. (In 1960, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration banned real sassafras in commercial root beer as safrole in high amounts was found to be carcinogenic.)

Throughout it all, zarza remained the dominant beverage of choice in and around the town of its origin in Veracruz. The Flores family is no longer the only one making it, either: A Google Maps search will reveal no fewer than five other zarzaparilla businesses in the town of about 23 square miles (for comparison’s sake, Mexico City is estimated at 573 square miles, yet according to Google, unfortunately has no official zarzaparilla-dedicated outlets).

Travel attractions in Teocelo

Teocelo has other worthwhile features besides zarza: It’s the site of the Fiesta Patronal, a weekend-long celebration that includes parades, fireworks and religious celebrations in honor of the burial of Jesus after his crucifixion. At the pueblo’s main entrance, there’s a bee sanctuary that produces all kinds of honey products you likely won’t find anywhere else, at least not in abundance — jugs of honey wine, salsa macha made with honey and “honey butter” (akin to peanut butter, with a similarly thick consistency) in variations that range from almond and walnut to berry or garlic.

Note: The honey shop, known as La Mielada, or “The Honeydew,” also has an accompanying restaurant that serves honeyed meats and breads, with an affordable selection of beverages like the aforementioned honey wine or my personal favorite, a mug of locally cultivated coffee with large dollops of organic honey mixed in — a pure delight of sweet and bitter flavors. For outdoor-seeking adventurers, the surrounding area also offers waterfalls, hikes, cabins and whitewater rapids.

To be sure, there’s no shortage of offerings — and mugs of zarza — to enjoy for a weekend in the chilly mountain locale.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: The hottest product on the planet is increasingly made in Mexico: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Let’s start today’s column with a quick quiz:

Pop Quiz Question #1: What is currently the top Mexican export to the United States?

If you are like most people, you are thinking of one of three categories: alcoholic beverages (think tequila, mezcal, Corona beer), food (perhaps avocados, jalapenos, tomatoes) or automobiles. All of those answers are incorrect.

Pop Quiz Question #2: Which country sells more AI servers and equipment to the United States, Mexico or Taiwan?

Of course, most people answer Taiwan. That would also be incorrect.

Mexico’s server-related exports to the US have overtaken autos, underscoring how AI data-center demand is reshaping its export base. Source: @financialtimes https://t.co/QtrH6mKZ0I pic.twitter.com/pyRYc40ktb — (((The Daily Shot))) (@SoberLook) August 7, 2026

Sometimes just one picture, or in this case — one chart recently published by the Financial Times — can be incredibly insightful. Above, you’ll see a chart comparing Mexican exports of two product categories from 2010 to the present day. The blue line shows vehicles, which Mexico has been exporting for over 60 years. Last year, nearly 80% of Mexico’s light vehicle exports went to the United States. The red line shows server-related hardware (think AI data centers). The x-axis shows the years from 2010 to 2026. The y-axis shows monthly exports in billions of US dollars.

As can be clearly seen, exports of server-related hardware have absolutely exploded in the past two years, to the point where they are now surpassing vehicles. Last month alone, over US $15 billion of these products were exported. Think about that for a minute. The news is filled on a daily basis with headlines telling us that Trump has decided not to renew the USMCA or that Trump commented that “we don’t need anything that Mexico has.” Other headlines lead us to believe that tariffs are being slapped on most Mexican goods, significantly hurting Mexico in the process. Neither is true.

That being said, much of the conversation often seems to revolve around two categories of products highly influenced by two distinct voting groups in the U.S. The first is union members and more specifically the members of the United Auto Workers, who have an obvious interest in keeping as much vehicle production as possible in the country. The second is U.S. farmers, who naturally want to keep food production domestic. As a result of these two powerful and influential groups, those segments are what we most often hear about — more specifically cars and tomatoes. And in fact, the U.S. currently has a 17% “antidumping” tariff on Mexican tomatoes and a relatively small and extremely complex-to-calculate tariff on Mexican vehicles. Fun fact: One of the final projects my senior year of college was to analyze the impact of U.S. tomato tariff practices and policies on Mexico. (Yes, I am aware of what an exceptionally boring topic that is for a final project!)

Perhaps not surprisingly, server equipment from Mexico has a 0% tariff from the United States. The most in-demand product on the planet right now has firmly established Mexico in its supply chain, and investment, jobs and exports are all booming in this area. Taiwanese companies are investing heavily in Mexico. It’s all happening very fast. It’s quite exciting and going to be very interesting to continue to follow.

So while most headlines would have you believe that the Mexico-U.S. trade relationship is in shambles, the reality is as follows:

1. Mexico moves past Taiwan as the top AI server exporter to the U.S.: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/business/mexico-moves-past-taiwan-as-top-ai-server-exporter-to-united-states/

2. Mexico is now by far the leading exporter to the U.S.: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/business/mexico-in-numbers-mexico-exports-us-china-canada/

3. Inflation is now lower in Mexico than in the U.S. for the first time: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/business/inflation-mexico-lower-united-states-why-thats-such-a-big-deal-a-perspective-from-our-ceo/

4. Mexico’s export revenue is up 25% so far this year: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/news/mexico-export-revenue-this-year/

So what’s the bottom line here? Follow the data, not the noise, and stay tuned to what is the most dynamic segment in the world, growing fast and furious right here in Mexico.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Costa Rica Court Questions Tourism Projects on Public Forest Land
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Constitutional Chamber will examine whether some tourism projects allowed on state-owned forest land should continue to be classified as low-impact activities. The case challenges rules covering canopy tours, hanging bridges, observation platforms in trees, rappelling areas, campsites and tourist lodges. These projects can currently be authorized on certain public forest properties located outside national parks and other protected areas.

The challenge was filed by the Asociación Cívica de Hermosa, a community organization based in Playa Hermosa. It argues that the government regulations make it possible to build tourism infrastructure on environmentally sensitive public land without enough legal or scientific support.

The court accepted the case for review on Friday, August 21. It gave the Ministry of Environment and Energy, known as MINAE, and the Attorney General’s Office 15 days to submit their positions. Accepting the case does not mean the court agrees with the organization or has found the rules unconstitutional. It only means the judges believe the questions raised deserve a full review.

The disputed rules remain in effect while the case moves forward. No nationwide suspension of canopy tours, lodges or other tourism operations has been ordered. The disagreement centers on a 2010 government regulation explaining how Article 18 of Costa Rica’s Forestry Law should be applied. That law allows the government to authorize research, environmental education and ecotourism on land belonging to the country’s Natural Heritage.

Natural Heritage land generally includes forests, wetlands and other environmentally important properties owned by the state and managed by the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC). Some of this land is outside officially designated national parks and wildlife refuges.

The current regulation lists several activities that SINAC can authorize on these properties. They include walking trails, campsites, lookout points, canopy tours, hanging bridges, kayaking, recreational cycling, fishing and tourist lodges. The legal challenge does not target every activity on that list. It focuses on campsites, canopy tours, tree platforms, hanging bridges, rappelling, lodges and a broader category covering other activities considered compatible with the environment.

The association questions whether projects involving platforms, buildings and other structures should automatically fall under the definition of low-impact ecotourism. It argues that the regulation may allow more construction than lawmakers intended when they approved the Forestry Law.

Under the existing system, SINAC can issue permits allowing people, community groups or businesses to use parts of this land. These permits do not give applicants ownership of the property. The government can also cancel them when it believes doing so is necessary to protect the public interest.

Depending on the project, applicants may be required to submit environmental studies, plans for handling waste and estimates of how many visitors the area can safely support. The Constitutional Chamber will review the responses from MINAE and the Attorney General’s Office before deciding whether the disputed parts of the regulation comply with Costa Rica’s Constitution. The court has not announced when it expects to issue a final decision.

World.title: Costa Rica Asked to Explain Fishing Boats Seen in Puntarenas Estuary
World.content:
The appearance of two fishing boats in the Puntarenas estuary has led a Costa Rican ocean conservation advocate to ask authorities for more information about the vessels, their owners and why they entered the area. Jorge Serendero Hülssner, director of Fundación For the Oceans and a member of the Marine Commission of the Presidential Council on the Ocean, raised the concern in a recent opinion column.

Serendero described the two boats as being of Chinese origin and identified one as TUNG HAI 168. However, he did not accuse either vessel of illegal fishing or any other crime. Instead, he asked authorities to clarify who owns and operates the boats, where they came from, what permission they had to enter the estuary and whether they had previously fished or transferred catches elsewhere in the region.

Public vessel-tracking information reviewed after the alert adds an important complication. Global Fishing Watch and commercial tracking services list TUNG HAI 168 as operating under the Costa Rican flag, not the Chinese flag. The vessel is approximately 24 meters (79 feet) long.

Those databases do not publicly identify its owner or explain why it carries a Chinese name. A boat’s name, appearance or country of construction does not prove its current nationality or ownership. The second vessel mentioned by Serendero was not identified in the column.

The available information therefore does not establish that TUNG HAI 168 is a foreign vessel. It also does not answer whether the boat had the necessary fishing, port or navigation permits. The location has added to the calls for an official explanation. The Puntarenas estuary is part of a protected wetland created in 2001 and expanded in 2005 and 2006.

The area includes mangroves, mudflats and important breeding grounds for fish and other wildlife. Puntarenas is also the legal headquarters of the Costa Rican Fisheries and Aquaculture Institute (INCOPESCA), which regulates the country’s fishing industry.

Serendero used the sighting to raise a wider concern about Costa Rica’s ability to monitor fishing activity across its waters. Large fishing operations can remain at sea for months with help from fuel, supply and refrigerated cargo vessels. Some transfer their catch to other ships without returning to port, a practice known as transshipment.

Transshipment is not automatically illegal, however, international fisheries organizations warn that weak oversight can make it harder to determine where fish were caught and whether fishing rules were followed. The concern also extends beyond Costa Rica. Isla del Coco forms part of the Eastern Tropical Pacific Marine Corridor, known as CMAR. Costa Rica, Panama, Colombia and Ecuador created the regional initiative to coordinate protection of connected marine areas that include Cocos, Coiba, Malpelo, Gorgona and the Galápagos Islands.

Sharks, tuna, turtles, rays and whales regularly move between these areas, meaning fishing or environmental damage in one part of the region can affect marine life elsewhere. Costa Rica has improved some of its monitoring tools and shares tracking information for Costa Rican fishing vessels with Global Fishing Watch, while radar systems help authorities monitor waters around Isla del Coco. Those systems, however, do not by themselves establish who owns the two boats seen in Puntarenas or what authorization they had.

No public response addressing the specific vessels could be located from INCOPESCA or the National Coast Guard as of today. The central question remains straightforward: whether Costa Rican authorities can identify the boats, their operators and the reason they were inside the Puntarenas estuary.

World.title: Thousands of Dead Crabs Wash Ashore on Guanacaste Beaches
World.content:
Thousands of dead crabs have washed up along some of Guanacaste’s best-known beaches, and nobody yet knows why. The animals have turned up at Playa Conchal, Brasilito, Flamingo, Potrero, Playa Negra, Ocotal, Guacamaya and Carrillo — a stretch covering much of the province’s northern tourist coast. Photos and video circulating online show them piled along the tide line in places.

They appear to be Euphylax dovii, called jaiba mora here and known in English as a pelagic swimming crab. That detail matters more than it sounds. This is not a beach crab since it lives out in open water, often well offshore, and travels in large groups. So these crabs did not crawl onto the sand so something carried them there.

The most likely candidate is the ocean itself. Costa Rica is in an El Niño, and the Pacific off the coast is running much warmer than it should. Readings from the University of Costa Rica’s Oceanographic Information Module show some sectors sitting about 3°C (5.4°F) above normal, with warmth reaching down to roughly 100 meters (330 feet). In April the figure was close to 4°C (7.2°F) above the long-term average.

Warm water changes how currents move and Marine biologist Jeffrey Sibaja, a researcher at the university’s Center for Research in Marine Sciences and Limnology, has said large gatherings of this species have shown up before during El Niño years in the eastern tropical Pacific, and that shifting currents can push them toward shore, where they get stranded. One possibility is that the crabs had massed to breed before the water moved them the wrong way.

None of that is proven yet, and scientists have been careful to say so. Warm water is context, not a verdict and there is a striking parallel further south. In Ecuador, the same species has proliferated so heavily this year that fishing crews report it destroying or tangling more than 90% of their nets, a surge researchers there tie to the same El Niño warming.

Costa Rica has seen the species behave strangely during an El Niño before. Researchers working at Isla del Coco in May 2015 found large numbers of them in surface waters just as that El Niño was beginning. For anyone heading to these beaches in the next few days, the practical picture is straightforward.

Dead crustaceans on the sand are unpleasant and can smell, but no health advisory has been issued and no beach has been closed. Municipal crews typically clear this kind of material within a day or two. Samples and water data now go to the lab. Until those results come back, the cause remains open.

World.title: Robbery suspect leaves social security card at the crime scene, police catch two men hours later
World.content:
Robbery suspect leaves social security card at the crime scene, police catch two men hours later

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Two men were detained within hours of an armed robbery at a shop on Big Creek Road in Independence Village on Saturday afternoon.

Police received information of a robbery in progress around 2:30pm. On arrival, officers found a wallet on the floor containing a social security card and other items belonging to one of the assailants.

The shop attendant told police that two men barged into the shop. One pulled out a 9mm pistol and demanded cash while the other took the cash register pan containing an undisclosed amount of money.

Both men then left the shop in an SUV heading toward Belize City.

Coordinated information was sent to G13 personnel, who stopped and detained both suspects at the junction of George Town Village in the Stann Creek District. An undisclosed amount of money was recovered.

Police are continuing investigations.

World.title: Belize Coast Guard supports Pancotto Primary School through community service
World.content:
Belize Coast Guard supports Pancotto Primary School through community service

By Zoila Palma: Students of the Belize Coast Guard’s Petty Officer Class Three Course 01/2026 stepped outside the classroom to give back to the community through a service initiative at Pancotto Primary School in Sandhill Village.

As the school prepares to welcome students for the new academic year, the Coast Guard sailors assisted with painting and other improvements aimed at creating a better environment for students and staff.

The initiative forms part of the Coast Guard’s leadership development efforts, emphasizing teamwork, civic responsibility and service to others. The organization said the activity reinforces the understanding that service to country extends beyond maritime duties and into the communities it serves.

The Belize Coast Guard recognized its Training and Doctrine Command for incorporating community service into the professional development of sailors, while commending the course staff and students for putting the organization’s values into action.

World.title: BELTRAIDE showcases Belizean creatives and entrepreneurs at Climate Week 2026
World.content:
BELTRAIDE showcases Belizean creatives and entrepreneurs at Climate Week 2026

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Trade and Investment Development Service (BELTRAIDE) is participating in Climate Week 2026 in Punta Gorda, Toledo, highlighting the role of creativity, entrepreneurship and innovation in building a more sustainable economy.

As part of Orange Economy Day, BELTRAIDE is showcasing Belizean creatives and entrepreneurs who are combining culture, tradition and innovation to develop new economic opportunities.

Their work also emphasizes reducing waste and making better use of locally available resources.

BELTRAIDE is using the event to highlight the support available to entrepreneurs through business development, market access, export readiness and other services designed to help transform local ideas into sustainable businesses.

World.title: PUP San Ignacio-Santa Elena slate has no Councilor candidate from Santa Elena
World.content:
PUP San Ignacio-Santa Elena slate has no Councilor candidate from Santa Elena

By Zoila Palma: The PUP’s municipal slate for San Ignacio and Santa Elena is taking shape following the party’s delegate convention, but the final lineup has no councilor candidate from Santa Elena.

The convention was held to select the councilor candidates who will join mayoral candidate Aaron Mai on the PUP’s slate for the 2027 municipal election. A total of 217 delegates and alternates cast ballots, representing a 100 percent turnout.

Edel Espat topped the polls with 194 votes, followed by Matthew Preston with 192, Joe Awe with 142, Nadime Hegar with 130, Eliu Yacab with 118 and Nazim Lisbey with 110.

Lisbey secured the final spot after a coin toss was used to break his tie with Danielle Rodriguez, who also received 110 votes.

The results mean that neither Danielle Rodriguez nor Omar Rodriguez, who were the candidates from Santa Elena, secured a place on the final municipal slate.

Omar Rodriguez received 66 votes, while Danielle Rodriguez tied with Lisbey at 110 but lost the deciding coin toss.

The PUP’s San Ignacio-Santa Elena team will therefore enter the 2027 municipal race without a councilor candidate from Santa Elena.

World.title: No Santa Elena Councilor candidate selected as Omar and Danielle Rodriguez fall short at PUP Convention
World.content:
No Santa Elena Councilor candidate selected as Omar and Danielle Rodriguez fall short at PUP Convention

By Zoila Palma: No councilor candidate from Santa Elena was selected to the PUP’s municipal slate following the party’s convention in Cayo, where delegates voted to determine the team that will contest the 2027 municipal elections for San Ignacio and Santa Elena.

Of the nine candidates who contested the convention, six secured positions on the final slate. Edel Espat topped the polls with 194 votes, followed by Matthew Preston with 192, Joe Awe with 142, Nadime Hegar with 130, Eliu Yacab with 118 and Nazim Lisbey with 110 votes.

The results mean both Santa Elena candidates, Omar Rodriguez and Danielle Rodriguez, did not secure a spot on the PUP slate.

Rodriguez received 66 votes, while Danielle Rodriguez garnered 110 votes. Lisbey also received 110 votes, resulting in a tie that was settled by a coin toss, with Lisbey winning the deciding toss.

The outcome leaves Aaron Mai as the PUP’s mayoral candidate, with Edel Espat, Matthew Preston, Joe Awe, Nadime Hegar, Eliu Yacab and Nazim Lisbey joining him on the municipal team.

World.title: Aaron Mai and PUP San Ignacio and Santa Elena team sworn in
World.content:
Aaron Mai and PUP San Ignacio and Santa Elena team sworn in

By Zoila Palma: Aaron Mai has been officially sworn in as the People’s United Party (PUP) mayoral candidate following the party’s municipal convention in Cayo, where delegates selected the councilor candidates who will form part of the PUP’s slate for the 2027 municipal elections.

The convention recorded a 100 percent turnout, with all 217 delegates or alternates casting their ballots.

The results saw Edel Espat top the polls with 194 votes, followed by Matthew Preston with 192 and Joe Awe with 142 votes. Nadime Hegar received 130 votes, while Eliu Yacab secured 118 votes.

Nazim Lisbey and Danielle Rodriguez both received 110 votes, while Lawrence Lennan garnered 105 votes and Omar Rodriguez received 66 votes.

A coin toss was used to break the tie between Lisbey and Rodriguez, with Lisbey winning the deciding toss and securing a spot on the slate.

Joining mayoral candidate Aaron Mai on the PUP municipal slate will be Edel Espat, Matthew Preston, Joe Awe, Nadime Hegar, Eliu Yacab and Nazim Lisbey.

The team will now prepare for the 2027 municipal election as the PUP seeks to secure victory at the polls.

PUP Secretary General Collet Montejo expressed gratitude to all candidates who participated in the convention and congratulated Mai as the party’s mayoral candidate.

World.title: BDF assists La Immaculada RC with back-to-school preparations
World.content:
BDF assists La Immaculada RC with back-to-school preparations

By Zoila Palma: Members of the Belize Defence Force (BDF) assisted with preparations at La Immaculada RC School in Eyles Camp, Orange Walk District, on Friday, August 21, 2026, as the school gets ready to welcome students for the new academic year.

Soldiers from Gulf Company of the Second Infantry Battalion carried out pressure washing, painting and other renovations aimed at improving the school’s facilities and creating a more welcoming environment for students and staff.

The school provided the necessary equipment, while the BDF members contributed their time, skills and labour to complete the community service project.

The BDF said it remains committed to supporting communities whenever possible while balancing its operational responsibilities.

World.title: International News: Canadian Prime Minister calls new U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods a ‘miscalculation’
World.content:
International News: Canadian Prime Minister calls new U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods a ‘miscalculation’

By Zoila Palma: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has called the United States’ decision to impose steep new tariffs on Canadian goods a “miscalculation” after trade negotiations between the two countries collapsed late Friday.

The new 50% duties took effect at midnight, affecting a wide range of Canadian exports and escalating tensions between the two North American trading partners, NBC reports.

Carney said the negotiations broke down because of what he described as “uneconomic” and “unfair” demands from the Trump administration.

“In short, they asked too much, and they offered too little,” Carney said.

The tariffs affect an estimated $20 billion worth of U.S. imports from Canada, with products ranging from hockey sticks and building materials to liquor and certain clothing. Canada has announced retaliatory measures, with Carney saying the country will respond with tariffs targeting U.S. goods in sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics. Those measures are expected to take effect September 8.

Carney said the U.S. had introduced significant changes to its demands during the final hours of negotiations, including restrictions on Canada’s ability to pursue trade agreements with other countries.

World.title: Stray animal highway horror
World.content:
The mangled Mitsubishi Pajero involved in the August 15 crash on the May Pen to Williamsfield leg of Highway 2000.

TOLL GATE, Clarendon — A night of T20 cricket enjoyment at Sabina Park in Kingston just over a week ago almost ended in death for three people when the sport utility vehicle in which they were travelling back to Mandeville crashed into a cow that had wandered onto the May Pen to Williamsfield leg of Highway 2000 in pitch darkness.

Hopeton McCatty, the driver and owner of the Mitsubishi Pajero; his friend Wensworth Skeffery, a former Opposition senator; and Skeffery’s 24-year-old daughter were not injured, but the cow died in the August 15 collision that revived fears of the danger posed to life by stray animals on the high-speed road.

“We took my friend’s daughter to cricket for the first time and she enjoyed it; a very good game of cricket, a fantastic crowd. We left Sabina Park and went downtown then joined the toll road at Portmore,” McCatty told the Jamaica Observer.

“We were talking about the experience of interacting with people and how to be humble. We were cruising along. We came through the tolls at Portmore, Vineyards, and May Pen. We were approaching the last one at Toll Gate driving at about 103 kilometres per hour… I had on the high beam, because the road was dark. We were in the left lane and while talking Skeffery said ‘Cow!’ ” McCatty related.

“I spotted this animal coming onto the road, so I braked and swerved to the right and we really thought we had missed it, but the cow kept coming and we hit the cow. The two airbags [deployed] and I swerved back to the left to avoid the median in the road. I wasn’t even able to see what was in front of me and I stopped,” added McCatty.

On Saturday, TransJamaican Highway (TJH) Limited Chief Executive Officer Ivan Anderson told the Sunday Observer that he had received a report on the incident and raised concern about residents living along that section of the highway repeatedly cutting through the fencing to get to their homes after disembarking buses travelling along the highway.

“The fence in this location has been cut and repaired several times since the start of the year. Since the initial cutting we doubled the fencing in this location by adding hog wire to the barbed wire; it is being cut by persons coming off buses on the highway and going into the community,” Anderson said in a WhatsApp response.

He said TJH is now in the process of identifying the owner of the cow as the animal was tagged.

On September 13 last year a woman had to be rushed to hospital after cattle strayed onto the highway shortly after midnight, causing extensive damage to two vehicles, a Toyota Axio and a Toyota Tacoma, and injuring occupants.

At that time the highway was toll-free. But when TJH commenced charging on December 27, 2025 it assured motorists of a First-World roadway supported by 24-hour patrols and consistent maintenance.

“Our commitment is to deliver a safe, reliable, and efficient driving experience across this new section in a manner that is consistent with our offerings on all legs of the TransJam Highway’s network. In order to deliver these services sustainably, we will introduce a toll rate structure at both the Toll Gate-MainLine Toll Plaza and the Toll Gate-Ramp Toll Plaza,” TJH said in an Instagram post.

However, for McCatty, the issue of stray cattle was compounded by him not seeing any patrols near midnight, and for close to an hour after the collision.

“The scary part about it is that when the car hit the cow all the lights went, because the battery got dislodged completely. We were out there on the highway in complete darkness,” he said.

“I didn’t know if a truck was going to come and run straight into us; and there has been an incident before on the highway network where people died after having an accident and then an oncoming vehicle hit them,” he added.

He said he was relieved when a tow truck, en route to Mandeville, stopped at the accident scene and subsequently removed his vehicle.

“God is good, because a wrecker was passing and stopped and had on its hazard lights; that give us some sense of calm that people wouldn’t run up into us in the darkness,” he said.

“The car bonnet seemed to have cut the cow’s neck. It took us about an hour to get off the road. During that time other vehicles stopped, but we didn’t see anybody from the toll [company] patrolling,” added McCatty.

He said he returned to Clarendon the Sunday afternoon following the accident to report it.

“We filed a report at the Four Paths Police Station on Sunday afternoon, because Sunday morning I couldn’t miss church. I had to give God thanks. We came out with no wounds. I reported the accident to the insurance company and the vehicle is basically written off,” he explained.

Vice chairman of the National Road Safety Council Dr Lucien Jones said he previously engaged the National Road Operating and Constructing Company (NROCC) — which is responsible for overseeing the design, construction, and maintenance of Jamaica’s highways — about the danger of stray animals on the high-speed road.

“Having a stray animal on a road which provides for driving at a fairly high speed to enable people to get from point A to point B in a fairly short time and therefore aid in the whole transportation sector carrying goods and people across the country, poses a severe problem,” he said.

“We have had this issue before. We have had discussions about it with operators of the highway [and] NROCC. We have had remedial things done on the highway, because the primary problem, as I understand it, has to do with people breaking or stealing the wires [fencing] on the highway and thus allowing cows to enter into a guarded space,” added Jones.

He is calling for the municipal corporations across Jamaica to reinstitute animal pounds and remove stray animals from endangering road users.

“We have had discussions about the role of the owners and now to hear that there was a crash recently involving a cow and a vehicle, thank God nobody died. It again raises the issue of how well we are guarding the space across the country on the highways. Not only the East-West or the North-South, but the one going from May Pen up into Mandeville. It raises an important issue which was addressed recently in an Observer editorial,” Dr Jones said.

He argued that the municipal authorities have “a mandate to provide for and enable the leading of stray cattle into pounds and to prevent individuals from allowing this kind of very dangerous situation to continue”.

Jones pointed to statistics indicating that 214 people have died on the nation’s roads since the start of the year, compared to 242 for the corresponding period last year.

“I would once again appeal to those who are so empowered — the municipal authorities and NROCC — to make sure, either separately or jointly, that our highways are made free of any kind of animal straying onto the road,” he said.

Dr Jones also pointed to another worrying trend of motorists driving the wrong way on highways.

On August 13 Parton Buchanan, a 56-year-old resident of Blenheim district in Hanover, died in a crash after he reportedly drove the wrong way onto the Porus off-ramp section of the highway near Williamsfield.

“In those instances where people have gone off-ramp in the wrong direction, they did so to either escape paying the toll or they are not aware of [how to use] that particular part of the highway. [It] requires an increase in public education as to how in certain areas we use the highways and to get people to be aware of the dangers,” said Jones.

McCatty is hoping that another layer of safety will be added by illuminating sections of the highway.

“When you have no light out there it is completely dark. If we can have lights where the toll booths are, why can’t we have it along the toll road? I am not saying you should have lights three feet apart, but there should be more light on the road,” he said.

World.title: Take responsibility!
World.content:
An injured Moo Moo seen at the side of a section of Walks Road in Spanish Town, St Catherine, last Monday. She was euthanised last Wednesday after Veterinary Services Division professionals determined her injuries were too severe. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

JAMAICA needs more animal shelters, but livestock owners must stop abandoning their roaming, injured animals for the Government to fix, warned Dr Sophia Ramlal, director of the country’s veterinary services.

Her comments come in the wake of a recent case involving an injured cow, given the name Moo Moo by residents, that spent days at the side of a road in Spanish Town, St Catherine, after being struck by a vehicle, with no owner coming forward to claim her.

Dr Ramlal said while such cases are not common, they have occurred before and are a cause for concern given the dangers stray animals pose to motorists and the general public.

“The Cruelty to Animals Act would address basic welfare issues for animals, the Keeping of Animals Act as well, which speaks to how animals are supposed to be kept and basic things should be provided to them, et cetera. However, there is a need for more pounds in Jamaica. There is a need for the ability to move animals that are stray and ownerless. I want to say, it is usually an instance where we have animals that are ownerless, or owners are unwilling to come forward and claim the animals, as is the case with this cow [Moo Moo] I’m addressing. In those instances, there is a need for the ability to remove the animals from the space to determine what is to happen to them,” said Ramlal.

She noted that a handful of organisations are already performing work that extends beyond what their limited infrastructure can reasonably support.

“The Jamaica Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (JSPCA) does really fantastic work, but they are probably, along with a couple of other entities, they are tasked with doing almost national duties without necessarily the infrastructure, so we need to be looking at more shelters, shelters even that work during disasters,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Ramlal said the Government is actively working to tackle rising public safety risks, crop destruction, and traffic hazards caused by stray livestock and roaming animals. Most recently, the Clarendon Municipal Corporation developed a new 20-acre holding facility and retrofitted transport trucks to manage roaming cattle and stray animals.

While State intervention is paramount, Dr Ramlal made it clear that this should not be left up to the Government to assume responsibility for animals whose owners can be identified or are unwilling to come forward.

“In this recent case, yes, the Government had stepped in to mobilise the agency as a State to both treat with euthanasia as well as the disposal of the carcass. There is also the process, though, in law, that if injuries occur and the owners are found, that through the court system, a judge may determine what costs are applicable and so on and so forth. In this case [involving Moo Moo], the State had to step in to mobilise and treat with the euthanasia and the disposal of the carcass.

“It is the owner’s cost to cover. It ought to be. The journey, the treatment of the animal, the euthanasia of the animal, if the animals were moved to a pound, all of those things, it is set out in law where those costs would have to be borne by the owner,“ Ramlal told the

Sunday Observer. “But given the circumstances of this cow and given the time frame and the confirmation from the police that nobody had come forward to claim ownership of the animal, then the necessaries had to be done in really the interest of the cow to relieve pain and suffering and to treat with this matter.”

She stressed that greater partnership is needed between the Government, communities and animal owners to keep animals safe, urging the public to report instances of neglected animals as quickly as possible.

“More shelters are needed, but we also need persons who own animals to be responsible owners. They need to be kept confined, they need to be fed, they need to be watered, they need to have proper shelter, and they need to be able to live normal, happy, healthy lives,” said Ramlal.

“We are looking to update our legislation to talk about not just basic cruelty, but also how it is that all of these five freedoms can be embodied in our legislation. We talk about how animals should be kept, how they should be treated if you’re using animals for work or sport, those kinds of things are in train, as we really also want to look at strengthening the legislation,” she added.

Ramlal said the latest incident proves that more and more Jamaicans are looking out for animals and this is a welcome move.

“I think Jamaicans love animals. I think it is growing amongst us that. Look, animals are a part of our ecosystem. More and more Jamaicans are embracing what we like to call in the veterinary medical fraternity and the medical fraternity, the concept of one health. More and more, we Jamaicans see animals not just as pets, but as companions, as service animals. Jamaicans’ view on animals and their contribution to society is on a positive trajectory, and I think what we saw unfolding with this cow tells you that Jamaicans from all walks of life can appreciate that animals are living beings and that they need support and that they’re willing to jump in and roll up their sleeves and help,” said Ramlal, reminding citizens to report any incident of animal abuse or neglect.

World.title: Eager for more
World.content:
Bloom: On Earth As It Is In Heaven (2026) by Avree Walker is delivered by the NDTC during Sunday evening’s sold-out performance at Iberostar Resort in Montego Bay.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — A standing ovation and packed auditorium at Iberostar Rose Hall Resort, Sunday evening, was a signal to principals of the National Dance Theatre Company (NDTC) that Montego Bay is eager to play a larger role in its annual season of dance.

Enthralled by an evening of intense and beautifully choreographed pieces, the appreciative audience applauded heartily after each performance and were left appearing eager for more.

There were audible oohs and ahhs of amazement as members of the troupe twisted, twirled, leapt, and executed a range of intricate moves across the stage.

The show was also remarkable in that it was the first time ever in its 64-year history that the NDTC was closing its season in the second city.

As Montego Bay’s Mayor Richard Vernon explained, the show had a dual purpose: To assist local dance troupe First Dance Studios as it recovers from the impact of last October’s Hurricane Melissa and to fulfil NDTC’s Artistic Director Marlon D Simms’ long-held dream of bringing the event to St James.

“We’re happy to welcome the NDTC [to] the city of Montego Bay and I trust that this will not be, in the future, for the sake of Melissa, but for the sake of culture…” Vernon told the gathering Sunday night. “[T]his is real, sustainable and something we can look forward to.”

Also present was hotelier and Montego Bay Arts Council Chairman Josef Forstmayr, who said more of these events are needed in the western city.

“We have to work hard; Montego Bay is better than its reputation. We are not just about sun, sea, and sand. This is a place now that has a very solid demand for cultural entertainment more than reggae, and we need to make sure that we get our fair share,” he said. “As we can see tonight, we have the potential to make it a worthwhile and financially successful enterprise, and we all need to work together to get a proper theatre, to get a proper venue where we can host events of that nature; we deserve it.”

Forstmayr did not hold back in his assessment of the event.

“You can see the turnout; it’s a fantastic turnout. There is an energy here. It makes you proud and then to see world-famous choreography, Many Rivers to Cross by [Rex] Nettleford, I mean, performed exquisitely by the elite dancers, it’s a once-in-a-lifetime experience — it’s spectacular, it’s just amazing, I’m over the moon,” he said.

The production was a feast for the senses, with its striking backdrops, vibrant colours, and eye-catching costumes complementing choreography that was precisely synchronised.

“It was exciting, we were all transfixed by what was happening on-stage…[I]t was a well-executed event, and I am very happy that I came this evening and we are looking forward to more for Montego Bay,” vice-president of the Montego Bay Chamber of Commerce and Industry Nadine Spence shared.

Local architect Isiaa Madden was also among those captivated by the performance.

“I think it’s fantastic! I think this is a great addition for Montego Bay, and I hope they’ll be back soon so that I can use my Sunday evenings to come to something like this, because it was great,” she said.

The NDTC’s artistic director also hinted that the performance could mark the beginning of something bigger for the company and the city.

“Perhaps tonight is more than a historic first; perhaps it’s the beginning of a new tradition,” Simms said to roaring applause.

He went on to thank the city of Montego Bay for welcoming the company so warmly, for standing with First Dance Studios, and for showing so resoundingly that the arts have a vibrant home in western Jamaica.

The mayor touched on a long-standing challenge: The lack of a dedicated space for performances of this kind.

Fairfield Theatre now lies in ruins, leaving the city with few suitable venues.

“We have heard the call, as well, for a theatre in Montego Bay. I do not want us to take that lightly; we need it. We have many young talents and youngsters doing their bit right across Montego Bay,” Vernon said. “They need a place to express themselves on a Sunday evening like this so that the entire Montego Bay can come out and enjoy themselves.”

In a follow-up with the Jamaica Observer, Vernon explained how he believes such a facility could become a reality.

“We have property that we can use and we can look at it from two perspectives. One, we would make it be a Government approach and, two, it could be a joined-up approach with Government and private sector, and I am hoping for any of the approaches,” he said.

“At the moment we have property space to envision and to implement something like this; we just need the partnership to make it happen. We are not going to leave it at that, we are going to have the conversations with the relevant persons and see how best we can bring that into our space, because there is a need for it, not a want,” he charged.

World.title: Six years of sleepless nights
World.content:
Shakira Warmington and her son Ayoze WarmingtonPhotos: Naphtali junior

FOR Shakira Warmington, raising a child with rare genetic condition congenital hyperinsulinism has been an uphill battle peppered with sleepless nights, financial strain, fights for a place in the country’s school system, and at times, questions of whether she has the strength to keep going.

Her son, Ayoze Warmington, is just six years old with a condition that sees his pancreas making too much insulin, causing severe and dangerous drops in his blood sugar. His condition, she said, is so rare that he is the only child in Jamaica diagnosed with the disorder, which was confirmed by his medical doctor.

Shakira said her son became sick at six months old, experiencing seizures and what she described as minor strokes. However, she said it was not until he was one year old that doctors were able to identify the condition.

Since then, Ayoze’s parents have had to reshape their lives around his health.

“Having a child with a rare illness in Jamaica is very challenging for us. His care, medication, schooling — just being able to ensure that he has a normal life — it impacts my work, and we are not necessarily in a position where I can stay at home. Both of us [her and Ayoze’s father] do our nine-to-fives and we both still have to do jobs on the side in order to maintain his health,” said Shakira, who is a teacher.

She said maintaining Ayoze’s health comes at a steep cost, with the family spending approximately $100,000 or more monthly on his care, depending on his health status, while also taking care of their daughter and covering all other household expenses. Shakira said the situation had been a lot worse, as previously they had to pay $40,000 every two weeks to access the medication Ayoze needs. However, thankfully, through the Ministry of Health’s Compassionate Care Fund that cost is now fully covered for six months, providing much-needed relief.

But perhaps the most taxing associated challenge is the fact that Ayoze requires 24-hour care.

His mother told thevJamaica Observer that she uses a glucose monitor at least three times a day when he is healthy, and up to 10 times daily when he is ill. She said some days she has to stick him every hour, resulting in a lack of sleep that causes her hands to tremble due to exhaustion.

“Because he gets ill so often I have to be the one to take care of him, ensure that he’s fed correctly and he’s fed on time, because of the weight issues. He throws up a lot and so eating has to be calculated, otherwise he throws it all up — and that, too, affects the weight. He will lose five pounds in a week just like that. He will be healthy this week; next week, he’s not eating. And when he doesn’t eat, the sugar goes down, and the sugar levels have gone into the negatives sometimes,” she told thevSunday Observer.

“I am mother, counsellor, and nurse. Over the six-year period it has impacted my nerves. I shake because you have to watch him while he sleeps. He has to be fed in his sleep because, naturally, the sugars in our bodies go low while we sleep, and his are already going low so it means while he sleeps it is a high possibility that he dies in his sleep, so he has to be fed,” she said, her hands shaking as she spoke.

“We have to feed him using a syringe while he sleeps because he doesn’t want food, he wants sleep; but whether he wants it or not, he has to get it because you have to keep pumping his body with the food. There was a time when he was being fed every hour, and I’m the one feeding him every hour, so it means I’m not sleeping. I have to feed him throughout the night; I still have to wake up to go to work, function throughout the work[day], get things going, doing it all over again — and that is if he’s healthy enough,” she added.

She said the suggestion was made for her to purchase a Dexcom machine to monitor his glucose levels, but that is an extra cost they cannot afford, so she became the machine.

Beyond the home, Shakira said challenges also exist with regard to Ayoze’s access to education. She said after he completed basic school she struggled to find a primary school that would take him. She said Ayoze was rejected by 15 schools, which said they did not have the resources to facilitate him.

Thankfully, he has now been enrolled in a private school to start in September — another expense for the family. A shadow has also been approved by the Ministry of Education for her son but because the stipend for shadows is low, they had to promise the shadow more money to make the job more attractive.

Shakira also believes her son needs to be assessed for learning and psychological challenges, but after applying for the assessment to be done she said they were number 200 in line. The mother has also tried to get him registered with the Jamaica Council for Persons with Disabilities, so as to access benefits on offer, but experienced challenges.

“I can tell you that dealing with special needs in Jamaica, it edges you into insanity. I’ve gone through many stages of depression because it’s like every day I’m questioning, ‘How will I?’ There’s just always a list, and much of life is taken up by him. I don’t have a social life. I feel so alone. It really is just my family here — me, him, my daughter, his daddy, and our family.

“I’ve gone through stages of feeling as though maybe I didn’t do something as a mother, or my body didn’t do something. It takes that effect on you mentally as a parent and makes you say, ‘Oh, maybe I wasn’t enough,’ or ‘I didn’t produce enough of something, and that’s why he became ill,’ ” said Shakira.

“I have had to deal with that, telling myself that it’s not my fault, or it’s nobody’s fault why my own child is ill. It feels like we are well-rooted, good, upstanding citizens doing what we should do in our community, and when we seek to get help for our sick child, it’s hard,” a visibly exhausted Shakira told the Sunday Observer.

She said the option was presented for Ayoze to undergo surgery to remove his pancreas, but that is a cost she and his father cannot afford. She noted that the surgery is not a cure, because he would become diabetic, and she is not sure the family will be able to manage that.

Defeated, Shakira asked for help to provide her son with the best level of comfort and care. She said he currently sleeps on a mattress on the floor because she fears he will fall to the ground and hurt himself while having a seizure. She asked for assistance to get him a customised bed, install a railing in the bathroom for him to use, and financial assistance to help the family maintain his care

“I want a big bed that is comfy,” said young Ayoze.

He said he loves when his mother takes care of him but he does not like being sick because it makes him feel sad.

“I want to get better because if I get better I will be happy,” he told the Sunday Observer.

Highlighting the challenges parents often experience trying to advocate for their children, Shakira said more needs to be done to assist families with children who have special needs.

“Find out more from parents. Gather us parents who have varying challenges and various children with types of special needs and find out what our daily life looks like and how, as a government, you can put in place policies that help to keep those of us with children or family members with disabilities to have some sustainable ways to gain assistance or gain support for our children,” she appealed.

“Where a nine-to-five job is concerned, there have to be some policies and policy changes that will impact us as parents dealing with children with special needs.
